    #10590. BotPsy: On-Device Personal Assistant with a Sub-Billion-Parameter Agentic Language Model

    📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2156 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

    BotPsy: On-Device Personal Assistant with a Sub-Billion-Parameter Agentic Language Model

    📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2156 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, frontier cloud LLMs carry high operational costs that can fluctuate unexpectedly, and relying on such third-party models introduces vulnerabilities, as providers can modify, deny, or deprecate access at any time.
    • Recent findings suggest that tether AI Research introduces BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model introduce BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model designed for function calling and agentic workflows, built on top of Qwen3.5-0.8B and suitable for on-device deployment.
    • In a recent development, building upon the foundation of BotPsy, future development by Tether Data, S.A.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, frontier cloud LLMs carry high operational costs that can fluctuate unexpectedly, and relying on such third-party models introduces vulnerabilities, as providers can modify, deny, or deprecate access at any time. Furthermore, proprietary models offer limited customization for specific workflows, while posing risks to privacy, data control, and transparency. Besides, not every task demands frontier-level intelligence: small, specialized agents can be equally capable on specific tasks and significantly cheaper to run, since many routine or smaller workloads can be processed efficiently on-device. As intelligence per parameter continues to improve rapidly, we aim to stand at the forefront of this shift toward performant, privacy-focused, self-hosted models.

    Recent findings suggest that tether AI Research introduces BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model introduce BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model designed for function calling and agentic workflows, built on top of Qwen3.5-0.8B and suitable for on-device deployment. BotPsy is a "personal assistant" that uses tools to perform a variety of simple tasks for the user, in domains such as web search & research, travel & lifestyle, commerce & finance, business & customer operations, device & vehicle control, files & documents, calendar, and email & messaging. Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty. BotPsy achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) tool-use and agentic performance for its size, outperforming every model of up to 1.2B parameters that we tested (Figures 1 and 2). Designed for secure on-device workflows, it provides exceptional instruction-following reliability and efficiency while keeping user data private. As a small model, BotPsy still makes mistakes and is not intended for high-stakes use; please read the Intended Use and Limitations for more information.

    🤗 Model (safetensors)  |  📦 GGUFs (bf16, Q8, Q4).

    In a recent development, building upon the foundation of BotPsy, future development by Tether Data, S.A. de C.V. (“Tether AI Research”, “we”, “our”) will focus on expanding on-device agentic capabilities to seamlessly integrate with an even broader array of hardware and local services. Tether's Hypersearch will evolve to support more robust decentralized peer-to-peer (P2P) queries, further ensuring private, encrypted web searches that bypass corporate trackers. QVAC Fabric local fine-tuning mechanisms will be optimized to adapt more deeply to individual user preferences, workflows, and specialized tool environments. Future iterations will allow the smartphone interface to smoothly delegate heavy computational tasks to home PCs or trusted secure P2P nodes during offline-online transitions. Privacy protocols will be continuously strengthened to guarantee that all personal data, credentials, and decisions remain strictly on local hardware. Collaborative features will be introduced to allow secure agent-to-agent communication across trusted local networks without compromising user confidentiality. Ultimately, these advancements will solidify BotPsy as a fully autonomous, highly capable personal AI ecosystem that keeps people entirely in control of their digital lives.

    BotPsy is based on Qwen3.5-0.8B and is post-trained in four sequential stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), and two rounds of Reinforcement Learning (RL). Each stage uses the previous stage's best checkpoint as its starting point and benefits from a different learning signal: imitation of reference trajectories, the token distributions of much larger teacher models, and rule-based tool-calling rewards (see Figure 3).

    Our approach uses four stages of training, which learn from three types of signal: demonstrations, specialist teachers, and verifiable rewards.

    Learning from demonstrations (SFT).

    We first perform full-parameter supervised fine-tuning on tool-use conversations. These include multi-turn agent trajectories from simulated environments, replayed single, parallel and multi-step calls, and cases where no tool should be called.

    Next, the student is trained with on-policy distillation (OPD): it generates its own responses, and a specialist teacher provides feedback on every token, using the per-token reverse KL divergence as the training signal. To build the teachers, we first RL-trained three Qwen3.5-4B models to specialize in tool use, general reasoning, and instruction following. During training, every prompt is routed to one of these teachers. This stage mainly aims to recover knowledge and instruction following, which degraded during the SFT stage, although the tool-use metrics also increase (see Figure 4).

    Learning from rules and environments (RL stages).

    According to recent reports, finally, the model is trained with reinforcement learning using DAPO [1], learning only from rewards computed by rules and verifiers. The first round focuses on tool calling, accompanied by instruction following and STEM multiple-choice questions. As in Tool-N1 [2], the tool-calling reward first checks the reasoning and tool-call format. Instead of Tool-N1's binary correctness reward, however, it gives fine-grained partial credit in the spirit of ToolRL [3], matching the predicted tool names, argument names, and argument values against the ground truth.

    Sources indicate that the second round widens the training mix to general-domain verifiable tasks: math, code, knowledge (multiple-choice) questions, instruction following, structured outputs, and multi-step tool use in a simulated workplace environment. Although this mix contains no multi-turn conversations, it further improves multi-turn function calling.

    Each stage of training uses a different data mixture (Figure 5). The SFT stage focuses mainly on tool use and prepares the ground for the subsequent stages. The MOPD mixture combines tool-use, knowledge and instruction-following data, both to further improve function calling and to recover the general-domain regressions from the SFT stage. The first RL stage again focuses mainly on tool use, while the second RL stage shifts the balance toward general-domain data (instruction following, knowledge, math and code), keeping a smaller share of tool use.

    BotPsy roughly doubles the tool-use performance of its Qwen3.5-0.8B base and is the strongest of the five models on five of the six agentic benchmarks: BFCL v4 (44.0 vs 23.4), ACEBench (58.7 vs 30.1), τ-bench (51.5 vs 23.2), BrowseComp-Plus (4.5 vs 1.9) and ToolSandbox (64.6 vs 30.5). On all five, it is also ahead of Qwen3.5-2B-Think, a model 2.5× its size (37.7, 55.4, 46.5, 2.8 and 41.2 respectively; see Table 1). On Claw-Eval, Qwen3.5-2B-Think leads (48.9 vs 46.5).

    Recent findings suggest that table 1: Tool-use and agentic benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined; multipliers give parameter count relative to BotPsy-0.8B. The average is the unweighted mean of the six benchmarks. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

    Tool-use training did not cost general knowledge: GPQA Diamond rises from 33.2 to 38.1 and MMLU-Pro from 41.6 to 48.9, the best of the models at 1.2B parameters or below (LFM2.5-1.2B-Think: 35.0 and 39.4; MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 15.8 and 40.0). Knowledge still scales mainly with parameter count, and Qwen3.5-2B-Think scores well above (59.9 and 65.5). BotPsy is therefore designed to call tools for facts it does not know, not to serve as a knowledge model.

    Table 2: General-knowledge benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

    BotPsy is the best of the five at following explicit instructions: IFEval 90.8 (base 59.7; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 80.0) and IFBench 55.9 (base 22.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 40.9). On Multi-IF, which tests instruction following over three turns in eight languages, it scores 67.2, on par with Qwen3.5-2B-Think (66.9) and LFM2.5-1.2B-Think (68.2). It starts strongest (84.3 in turn 1, the highest of the five) but drops faster as instructions accumulate (51.0 in turn 3, vs 56.5 and 56.2 for those two models). Lower-resource languages remain a weakness: Hindi (24.5) and Russian (57.6) are far below the 72–80 reached in English, Chinese, French, Spanish, Italian and Portuguese.

    Table 3: Instruction-following benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

    Industry observers note that the largest relative gains come in multi-turn, stateful interaction, where BotPsy leads four of the five multi-turn benchmarks (Figure 6). On BFCL v4 multi-turn it rises from 7.5 to 46.1, nearly double Qwen3.5-2B-Think (23.8), and on ACEBench Agent from 7.9 to 28.3 (Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 16.2). On τ²-bench it doubles its base in retail (67.8 vs 33.9, a narrow lead over Qwen3.5-2B-Think at 65.5) and reaches 82.5 in telecom, where the agent has to guide a user through troubleshooting over many turns (MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 74.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 69.3). It is also the most reliable of the five at single calls (BFCL non-live: 83.0) and at not calling a tool when none fits (BFCL hallucination: 86.1).

    Recent findings suggest that botPsy's weaker spots are open-ended search and a few areas where Qwen3.5-2B-Think still leads. BotPsy's BrowseComp-Plus score of 4.5 is the best of the five, but low in absolute terms, and on BFCL web search (14.0) and memory (16.3) it trails Qwen3.5-2B-Think (19.8 and 26.1). On Claw-Eval, BotPsy improves clearly on its base (46.5 vs 39.3) but remains slightly below Qwen3.5-2B-Think (48.9). On ACEBench's special cases (incomplete or erroneous requests), Qwen3.5-2B-Think is also ahead (58.0 vs 51.3), although BotPsy is far above its base there (13.7). τ³-banking is the one multi-turn benchmark where BotPsy does not lead: no model gets above 5 (BotPsy 4.1, unchanged from its base; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 4.8).

    BotPsy can handle a variety of use cases and scenarios. Figure 7 breaks the benchmark scenarios down by app group, separating simple scenarios (single turn, one tool call) from complex ones (multi-turn or multi-tool). The overall scores quoted in this section are averaged over all scenarios; the bottom row of Figure 7 is an unweighted mean of the seven groups, so its numbers differ.

    Simple scenarios score 70–79 in every app group with a meaningful sample (Communication & Social has only 6). Overall, BotPsy scores 75, about 21 points above its base model (54) and slightly above Qwen3.5-2B-Think (70).

    On complex scenarios, BotPsy scores 39.5 overall, against 17.9 for its base and 30.8 for Qwen3.5-2B-Think. The gain is largest in Communication & Social (61 vs 13 for the base), Commerce & Services (58 vs 27) and Device & System Management (46 vs 15). Qwen3.5-2B-Think is ahead only in Personal Productivity & Work (64 vs 58, 38 scenarios, mostly Claw-Eval), and MiniCPM5-1B-Think is marginally ahead in Communication & Social (61.5 vs 60.5). Multi-step tasks still score lower than single calls, which remains the main limit for harder tasks.

    Complex Information Retrieval & Research scenarios score 15 (single calls: 79). Most are BrowseComp-Plus deep-research questions, which stay hard for every model in this size range (base: 9; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 14).

    BotPsy reaches correct answers with much less reasoning than its base, and with fewer turns on multi-turn agent tasks. This aligns with our explicit focus on reasoning efficiency throughout training. All comparisons below are made on the same questions or tasks (those that all five models answered correctly or solved), so differences in difficulty do not drive the numbers. Reasoning tokens are counted with each model's own tokenizer.

    Shorter reasoning, with higher accuracy. Compared with its base, BotPsy uses 1.4–3.1× fewer reasoning tokens per correct answer on GPQA Diamond (3,690 vs 11,563), MMLU-Pro (1,912 vs 5,105), IFEval (3,148 vs 4,433) and IFBench (4,204 vs 11,576), while scoring higher on all four (Figure 8). It is not the shortest model everywhere: LFM2.5-1.2B-Think writes shorter reasoning on MMLU-Pro, IFEval and IFBench, and MiniCPM5-1B-Think on IFEval and IFBench, but at lower accuracy than BotPsy on each.

    Fewer turns than the base on multi-turn agent tasks. On τ²-bench tasks that all five models solve, BotPsy needs fewer assistant turns than its base (Figure 9):.

    According to recent reports, it does this while passing 2.0× (retail) and 2.6× (telecom) as many tasks as the base. MiniCPM5-1B-Think uses fewer turns on retail (8.7), but passes only 9.9% of retail tasks.

    Industry observers note that botPsy has been developed to advance the state of the art and to support research and educational uses. Models developed based on our work could be suitable for tasks in domains such as device & system management (settings, files & documents, clocks & alarms), personal productivity & work (calendar & tasks, email, collaboration tools), communication (messaging), information retrieval & research (web search, weather, news), media & lifestyle (video, music, recipes & fitness, photos) and commerce & services (maps & travel, finance, shopping & delivery). Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty.

    Industry observers note that botPsy has been primarily trained and tested in English, which is the recommended language. It has also been evaluated on Multi-IF, which covers seven additional languages (Chinese, French, Hindi, Italian, Portuguese, Russian and Spanish): it performs well in most of them, but scores much lower in Hindi and Russian. BotPsy is a small language model, and it makes mistakes. It is not intended for safety-critical or high-stakes automated decisions, or for applications involving money, personal information, health and other sensitive topics.

    [3] Qian, Cheng, et al. "ToolRL: Reward is All Tool Learning Needs." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 (2025).

    #10589. How to sign transactions from your backend without exposing the private key

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (609 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

    How to sign transactions from your backend without exposing the private key

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (609 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Keep the private key out of your backend entirely.
    • The way most people start is with a private key in an environment variable and a script that signs locally.
    • They differ in what stands between a compromised backend and a signature.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Keep the private key out of your backend entirely. Put it in a signer your backend calls, and put the rule that decides each signature next to the key instead of in your server. On Lit Protocol the key lives inside a secure enclave, and the rule is a Lit Action, a JavaScript function that runs in that enclave before every signature. Your backend gets an API key that can only request signatures. If someone breaks into your backend, they can ask for signatures that pass your rule, and that is all they can do.

    The way most people start is with a private key in an environment variable and a script that signs locally. I understand why. It works and it is fast to set up. The problem is that anything with access to that process can read the key. And there is nothing between the script's logic and the signature, so a bug in the strategy becomes a signed transaction.

    There are four common designs. They differ in what stands between a compromised backend and a signature.

    The first is a cloud KMS like AWS KMS. The key stays in the HSM and your backend asks it to sign a hash. Nothing stands between your backend and a signature except IAM permissions. The KMS does not know what a blockchain transaction is.

    The second is a hosted signer with a policy engine. The provider holds the key and checks your allowlists and caps before signing. The rule can see the transaction fields. It cannot see your ledger, a price, or whether a deposit landed on another chain.

    Recent findings suggest that the third is a rule written as code that runs inside the enclave with the key. The rule can fetch whatever it needs. This is how Lit works.

    The fourth is a smart account with modules. A Safe or an ERC-4337 account enforces the rule on-chain. This is fully public, but it costs gas per operation, it only works on EVM chains, and the rule can only use data that is already on-chain.

    This Lit Action signs a settlement only after it confirms the deposit on the source chain.

    Your backend calls it like this, using the execute-only key.

    Sources indicate that when the request comes in, the enclave hashes the code and checks that your API key is allowed to run that hash against that wallet. Then it runs the function and returns the signed transaction. Lit's code never sends the key out of the enclave, and only the actions in the wallet's group can use it.

    It has been revealed that it cannot create a wallet, add a rule, or change a group. Those actions need your account key. If you use ChainSecured mode, they need a transaction from the wallet that owns your account on Base. Keep both of those away from your production servers.

    Give each service its own execute-only key, scoped to one group. Put the amount cap and the destination check in the signer's rule, not just in your own code. Test revoking a key before you launch, and notice that the wallet address does not change when you do. Keep the wallet's balance at a working level. A rule stops signatures that break the rule. It cannot undo a mistake that the rule allowed.

    According to recent reports, to create an account, go to the Lit dashboard and click Create an account. The API reference is at developer.litprotocol.com/management/api_direct.

    Sources indicate that this is part 3 of a five-part series on building with Lit. Part 4 is about adding wallets to your app with an API.

    The Definitive Fine-Tuning Guide for 3D Generation Models

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2508 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • TLDR; In this blog, we provide fine-tuning scripts and containers to fine-tune TRELLIS.2, a popular 3D model on your 3D assets, that can run both locally and on Hugging Face Jobs.
    • 3D generation has many uses in robotics, simulation, media, and entertainment.
    • TRELLIS introduced a common internal representation, called a unified latent representation.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    TLDR; In this blog, we provide fine-tuning scripts and containers to fine-tune TRELLIS.2, a popular 3D model on your 3D assets, that can run both locally and on Hugging Face Jobs. If you are interested in fine-tuning, you can use our scripts with few arguments (assuming you updated your dataset to Hugging Face Hub) or tinker with them yourself with this repository. If you want to learn more, we go through how the script works. Let’s go!

    3D generation has many uses in robotics, simulation, media, and entertainment. In these fields, it is difficult to make generated objects obey strict rules and standardize model and data representations. There are many file formats, such as GLB and PLY. There are also many representations, such as neural radiance fields (NeRFs) and 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS). Each one has different advantages and disadvantages.

    TRELLIS introduced a common internal representation, called a unified latent representation. Its decoders convert this representation into 3D models in the required output format. Thus, you do not have to use different models for each representation format.

    The same team then released TRELLIS.2, which improves the model's representation of 3D structure. But neither model gives an easy way to adapt it to a specific task.

    According to recent reports, A general-purpose model, such as TRELLIS.2, can make errors in details that are vital for a specific application. For example, a user may need accurate geometry for furniture models. Without fine-tuning for that task, the pretrained model can produce geometry that is insufficiently accurate. We use a subset of GSO that has 188 footwear objects for our experiment. In our initial tests, the pretrained model usually produced shoes that looked correct, but the soles were incorrect. We test whether a LoRA can make the soles more accurate.

    In a recent development, our goal is to use the Google Scanned Objects (GSO) dataset to improve the performance of TRELLIS.2 on a specific object category. We will explain which pipeline components to fine-tune and which to leave unchanged during training. The pipeline separates structure, detailed geometry, and materials. Thus, we will fine-tune only the components that are notable for our task.

    Choosing what to freeze matters as much as choosing what to fine-tune.

    LoRA, short for low-rank adaptation, fine-tunes a model by training small adapter matrices while keeping the original weights frozen. This reduces the number of trainable parameters and the memory needed for their gradients and optimizer state. We use Hugging Face’s PEFT library to add and train these adapters. For more information, read our LoRA guide.

    In a recent development, hugging Face Jobs runs containerized workloads on cloud hardware. We use it for preprocessing and for training. To use your own GPU instead, see the local Docker commands below. Before you start, make sure that you have:.

    Before we train, let’s look at how TRELLIS.2 generates a 3D object and where we’ll add LoRA adapters.

    TRELLIS.2 has five main stages: remove the image background, encode the image, predict the coarse structure, generate detailed geometry, and generate materials. The pipeline then exports the result as a textured mesh.

    In a recent development, first, BiRefNet removes the background from the input image. DINOv3-L then encodes the image into feature tokens. The generation models use these tokens to guide the 3D object.

    The sparse-structure flow DiT predicts the object's coarse shape. It is a diffusion transformer (DiT) that makes a small latent of size 16³ × 8. A variational autoencoder (VAE) decoder then changes this latent into a 64 × 64 × 64 occupancy grid. Each voxel in the grid shows if that location is part of the object. A voxel is a pixel in three dimensions. We add LoRA adapters to this model because its output guides the geometry stage.

    Industry observers note that O-Voxel is the 3D format of TRELLIS.2. It is a sparse voxel grid. It keeps only the voxels on the object's surface. Each voxel keeps local geometry, such as a mesh vertex, and material attributes. Because the format is small, a CPU changes a mesh into O-Voxel in seconds. A GPU changes O-Voxel back into a mesh in seconds.

    Structured sparse latents come from TRELLIS. They keep 3D data in sparse tensors, which makes computation faster. The model uses only approximately 10% of the voxels in the grid, so it does not spend compute on empty voxels. Thus, the shape flow DiT and the texture flow DiT are sparse transformers. The sparse-structure flow DiT is a dense transformer.

    The shape flow DiT uses the occupancy grid and the DINOv3 feature tokens to make a latent. Another VAE decoder then changes this latent into O-Voxel geometry at a resolution of 512 × 512 × 512.

    We add LoRA adapters to the DiT at this stage because it controls the object's shape.

    In the last stage, the texture flow DiT uses the shape latent and the DINOv3 features as input. It defines the materials and textures of the geometry's surface. A VAE decoder then changes the latent into base color, metallic, roughness, and alpha values for each voxel. We do not add LoRA adapters to this stage. Our dataset has diffuse color maps, but it lacks the separate material maps this stage needs for training. Also, our problem is the shoe's shape. The base model already makes good colors and textures.

    Finally, the pipeline combines the geometry and material attributes into a textured mesh and exports it as a GLB file.

    Industry observers note that we add LoRA adapters only to the sparse-structure flow DiT and the shape flow DiT. These DiTs control the object's shape and geometry. We freeze the texture flow DiT to keep its current capabilities.

    Our dataset contains diffuse color maps that include baked lighting effects. To train the texture flow DiT, we need separate material maps. The color maps in our dataset mix surface color with lighting. Thus, they are not correct targets for this training.

    If we train the texture flow DiT on these maps, it can learn to show lighting as a surface property. It can also forget what it learned before, a problem called catastrophic forgetting.

    In a recent development, our subset has 188 shoes from the 1,030 objects in GSO. For a dataset this small, LoRA is a better choice than full fine-tuning. Full fine-tuning costs much more. It can also overwrite what the model already does well (its learned priors). Our configuration trains approximately 9.3 million adapter parameters in total for both targeted DiTs. We use rank 8 adapters in the attention and feed-forward (MLP) layers of the sparse-structure flow DiT. We use rank 16 adapters in the attention layers of the shape flow DiT. The rank sets the size of the adapter matrices. A higher rank lets the adapter learn more.

    A 3D model setup can need many dependencies and installation steps. We supply two Docker images (that you can run on Jobs or your own machine) with the necessary software. One image is for preprocessing, and one is for fine-tuning.

    To train your LoRA adapters and upload them to the Hub:.

    Then we explain the fine-tuning script, its settings, and how each setting affects training.

    We’ll walk through three parts of the experiment:.

    We save the preprocessed dataset so that all training runs can reuse it.

    The preprocessing container uses Blender to render 16 views of each object. LoRA training will use these views as conditioning images. Blender runs without a display, through the xvfb-run utility. The container also processes each object through the preprocessing pipeline. See the footwear dataset here for an example intermediate output. For our 188 objects, the full run took approximately 1 hour on an a100-large job. A compact version of the preprocessing pipeline is also available in this companion repository.

    For Hugging Face Jobs, we pass the following arguments:.

    This container accepts a few more arguments (regardless of being run on Hugging Face Jobs or with Docker), that you can find documented over here. The steps taken in the preprocessing pipeline are documented in this section later.

    It has been revealed that the training container loads the prepared dataset and a configuration preset or file. It records training metrics with Trackio. Use the Trackio dashboard to monitor the run.

    Recent findings suggest that we use ‘ss’ and ‘shape’ to indicate the two modes we have for training the LoRAs. The ‘ss’ mode will finetune only the Sparse-Structure Flow DiT, whereas the ‘shape’ mode will finetune the Shape Flow DiT. Under the hood, they simply reference different config.json files to use for each stage. More details about the process is available in this section later.

    In a recent development, if you set --push-to, the container uploads adapter checkpoints to the Hub. The container accepts parameters that are also documented here for brevity. A compact script is also available in the same repository.

    If you want to play around and fine-tune with the already-processed dataset we have, feel free to use the following set of commands.

    Industry observers note that the commands and flags are the same as for Hugging Face Jobs. Only the Docker options are different.

    If you want to use our already-preprocessed dataset locally on your machine of choice, use the following commands:.

    Our trained LoRA adapters are in this repository: suvadityamuk/trellis-2-finetune-gso.

    We use TRELLIS.2’s frozen encoders to convert the input meshes into training latents. We save these latents, so later runs do not have to encode the meshes again.

    We also render 16 views of each object in Blender. During training, we select one random view for each sample as the conditioning image. We keep 9 of the 188 objects for evaluation and train on the other 179. These held-out objects show whether the adapters work on objects unseen by the model during training.

    Some of the views that Blender rendered for one object.

    In a recent development, the first snippet sets up the data. FLOW selects the flow DiT to train (ss or shape), and STEPS sets the number of optimizer steps. A batch size of 4 with 4 gradient accumulation steps gives an effective batch size of 16. Then, the snippet loads the LoRA config file for the selected flow DiT, makes the dataset in the TRELLIS.2 format, removes the held-out objects, and makes the data loader for fine-tuning.

    We use the peft library to insert LoRA adapters into the selected layers. TRELLIS.2 has a custom forward pass, so the standard PeftModel() wrapper does not work. Instead, we call inject_adapter_in_model(). This function adds the adapters directly to the model and keeps its custom interface.

    Sources indicate that we keep the trainable adapter weights in 32-bit floating point (fp32) for numerical stability and use bfloat16 (bf16) autocasting for the forward pass. Autocasting lets PyTorch use lower precision for some operations, which decreases memory use. Autocasting does not change how the frozen backbone weights are stored.

    According to recent reports, it’s key to note that our objective function here is good-old rectified flow matching (as seen in popular image-generation models like Stable Diffusion 3, Flux 2, and others). TRELLIS.2 used the same objective in pretraining, so it is a good choice for fine-tuning. For the theory, read this blog about flow matching.

    We upgrade only the LoRA parameters in the sparse-structure and shape DiTs. All original model weights remain frozen.

    Recent findings suggest that the snippets below show the core training loop for one stage. They are simpler than the container code and do not include some setup steps. For the full workflow, use the container commands.

    We initialize the optimizer and load DINOv3 to extract features from the input images.

    We then follow these steps within the training loop:.

    Sources indicate that the training loop computes the loss and updates the adapter weights. Gradient accumulation adds the gradients from 4 small batches before each optimizer step. Gradient checkpointing saves GPU memory by recomputing some intermediate values during backpropagation. The outer loop runs for a given number of optimizer steps, whereas the inner loop accumulates gradients over a set of batches.

    For each batch, DINOv3 encodes the conditioning image. For classifier-free guidance (CFG) dropout, the loop sets the conditioning to zero for a random fraction (p_uncond) of the samples. Then, it calculates the flow-matching loss with bf16 autocasting. After the inner loop, it clips the gradients to prevent very large updates and does an optimizer step. It logs the loss every 10 steps and saves an adapter checkpoint every 500 steps.

    We trained two adapters: one for the sparse-structure DiT and one for the shape DiT. The LoRA config files in the container image contain the full training settings: ss_flow_lora_gso.json for the sparse-structure flow DiT and slat_flow_img2shape_lora_gso.json for the shape flow DiT. Each run used one A100 80 GB on Hugging Face Jobs. The sparse-structure run took 7.2 hours, and the shape run took 3.6 hours.

    Industry observers note that the training loss of the sparse-structure flow DiT falls promptly at the start, then more slowly. The loss of the shape flow DiT stays at approximately the same level. These curves show how the training objective changes, but they do not directly measure the quality of the generated geometry.

    It has been revealed that flow-matching loss varies with the sampled objects, noise, and timesteps. To find out if fine-tuning improves the geometry, we must also compare outputs on the held-out objects.

    Sources indicate that the figure below compares outputs for five of the nine held-out objects. It highlights the input image, the base model’s generated output, the base output after a rotation adjustment, the output with the footwear adapters, and the reference scan. In these examples, the soles from the fine-tuned model are closer to the scans.

    We also use three metrics to evaluate the geometry on the test set:.

    In the chart’s nine-object comparison, the base model has a mean F-score of 0.276, compared with 0.803 for the model with the footwear adapters. Chamfer distance falls from 0.174 to 0.033, and normal consistency rises from 0.530 to 0.804. With both adapters, the F-score is better on all nine held-out objects.

    For the statistics of all runs, see this Trackio space.

    Industry observers note that phew, so there we go! We fine-tuned TRELLIS.2 for footwear generation by adding LoRA adapters to the two model components that control geometry. We prepared the data once, trained the adapters in separate jobs, and evaluated the outputs on held-out objects.

    The main lesson is to select a training target that agrees with the problem and the data that you have. For this experiment, we fine-tuned the structure and shape stages and froze the texture stage.

    Next, we can examine if the same choices help other 3D generation models, such as Pixal3D and UniLat3D.

    According to recent reports, gaussian-splat and world-generation models, such as HunyuanWorld 2.0 and NVIDIA Lyra 2.0, are also possible next steps. Their representations and training pipelines can need different methods.

    According to recent reports, thank you for following along, and see you in the next one! 👋🤗.

    #10583. Shipping a Database Index Without an Outage on WordPress VIP

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (985 w)

    Shipping a Database Index Without an Outage on WordPress VIP

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (985 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The deploy trap mentioned in passing in an earlier post — that an index hint referencing an index MySQL doesn't recognize yet is a hard error, not a slow query, so the index has to exist before the code that references it goes live — turns out to generalize well beyond that one sitemap fix.
    • It has been revealed that TL;DR: A shared plugin enhancement needed five new indexes across a multisite network.
    • Recent findings suggest that A shared plugin used across the network needed a version bump that included, among other things, five latest index-creation commands — covering things like sitemap last-modified lookups, taxonomy timestamps, and media MIME-type filtering, the same category of query-plan problem covered in the sitemap posts, just generalized into reusable commands rather than one-off fixes.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The deploy trap mentioned in passing in an earlier post — that an index hint referencing an index MySQL doesn't recognize yet is a hard error, not a slow query, so the index has to exist before the code that references it goes live — turns out to generalize well beyond that one sitemap fix. It came up again, differently, shipping a batch of five new indexes as part of an internal shared plugin upgrade across a WordPress VIP-style multisite network. This time the near-miss wasn't about sequencing an index against code. It was about trusting a diff.

    It has been revealed that TL;DR: A shared plugin enhancement needed five new indexes across a multisite network. The actual near-miss wasn't the indexes — it was applying a narrow version-bump diff to a branch that had silently drifted two minor versions further behind than assumed, landing a partial, subtly broken state. Fix: verify the base directly, replace the tree wholesale instead of trusting the diff, then apply the same existence-guard discipline to the index rollout itself.

    Recent findings suggest that A shared plugin used across the network needed a version bump that included, among other things, five latest index-creation commands — covering things like sitemap last-modified lookups, taxonomy timestamps, and media MIME-type filtering, the same category of query-plan problem covered in the sitemap posts, just generalized into reusable commands rather than one-off fixes. Each command follows the same shape: a status check to report whether the index already exists, and an ensure action to create it, safe to run repeatedly.

    According to recent reports, --network runs it against every site in the multisite install in one pass; --dry-run=false is deliberately required rather than defaulted, so an accidental invocation without it reports what would happen instead of mutating the schema. status afterward re-checks all five against both a staging and a production-mirrored environment before anything goes near real traffic.

    That part went cleanly. The near-miss happened one step earlier, validating the change on an intermediate branch before it ever reached the index commands.

    The plan was ordinary: bump the shared plugin from one version to the next, validate the bump on a develop branch first, then open the real pull request against main. The version bump itself — call it 4.21.3 to 4.21.4 — was a small, contained diff. Cherry-picking just that diff onto develop seemed like the lower-risk move: touch less, verify faster.

    develop's copy of the plugin wasn't actually at 4.21.3. It was pinned two minor versions further back, at 4.19.0 — a fact the diff itself gave no indication of, because a diff only describes the distance between the two versions it was generated from, not the version of whatever it's about to be applied to. Applying the narrow 4.21.3→4.21.4 diff on top of an actual 4.19.0 base landed exactly the changes that diff described and nothing else — silently skipping every change introduced in the two versions develop had missed in between, including includes and files the plugin's newer code now assumed existed.

    Sources indicate that the plugin didn't fail loudly. It failed the way missing includes usually do: warnings on load, behavior that's subtly wrong rather than obviously broken, the kind of state that's easy to wave off as noise during a validation pass if you're not specifically watching for it.

    Industry observers note that the fix, once caught, was to stop treating this as a diff-application problem and treat it as a state problem: replace the plugin directory wholesale with the exact tree from the released 4.21.4 version, rather than trying to reconstruct the missing intermediate changes by hand. Confirmed clean load with zero warnings afterward, and only then did the five index commands get run against it.

    It has been revealed that the specific bug — a stale branch, an unexpectedly large version gap — is mundane. What generalizes is the assumption underneath it: that a diff between version X and version Y is safe to apply anywhere, because the diff itself looks small and contained. A diff only knows about X and Y. It states nothing about the actual state of the branch you're about to apply it to, and if that branch silently drifted further behind than anyone tracked, a clean-looking small diff can land a broken partial state without raising any obvious alarm — no merge conflict, no failed patch, just missing files the new code quietly assumes are there.

    The generally safer default, once a branch's actual pinned version is in doubt: check what's actually there before deciding whether a diff or a full-tree replacement is the right move. A version pin is a claim about state, and claims about state are worth verifying directly rather than inferring from how major or small the intended change looks on paper.

    Once the code was confirmed correct, the index rollout followed the same discipline covered in the earlier sitemap post: never assume a referenced index exists just because the deploy that's supposed to create it has already shipped. The commands were run with an explicit status check both before and after ensure, against every site in the network individually, not just spot-checked on one — a network-wide --network flag makes it easy to assume uniform state across sites that may, in practice, have drifted from each other in exactly the way the branch above had.

    According to recent reports, that last point turned out to matter beyond this one rollout: the branch drift that caused the near-miss above was itself a symptom of develop having gone unsynced with main for longer than anyone had tracked, on a dependency pinned by another engineer's unrelated, still-open work. Fixing the immediate version mismatch doesn't fix that underlying drift — it's worth flagging as its own follow-up, separate from the deploy that surfaced it, rather than assuming one clean bump means the branches are back in sync generally.

    #10580. Terraform Applied Cleanly and Measured Nothing

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1078 w)

    Terraform Applied Cleanly and Measured Nothing

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1078 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, terraform apply reported nine checks created, no errors.
    • The scripts inside them run somewhere else entirely — on Grafana's probe machines, on their schedule, with no path back to your terminal.
    • You ask the data, because nothing else will tell you.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, terraform apply reported nine checks created, no errors. Which established exactly one thing: nine check definitions now exist in a vendor's database.

    The scripts inside them run somewhere else entirely — on Grafana's probe machines, on their schedule, with no path back to your terminal. A script that aborts on its first line produces an apply that looks identical to one that works. That gap, between configured and measuring, is where this system tried to fail three separate times.

    You ask the data, because nothing else will tell you.

    Industry observers note that the first armed run failed. Not visibly — the checks existed, the dashboard was drawn, terraform plan was clean. The failure was in the logs on the vendor's side:.

    In a recent development, that's the incomplete options block — a documentation snippet showing the browser fragment, copied as though it were a whole options object. The point here isn't the fix. It's that Terraform had done its job perfectly and the system was measuring nothing, and there is no arrangement of proposal, apply, or state inspection that would have noted so.

    So a template change gets three checks afterward, in Explore:.

    and the errors themselves in Loki:.

    Recent findings suggest that the middle one is the load-bearing query. probe_success can be 1 for a check whose script threw after navigating — the run completed, the vendor is satisfied, and no vital was recorded. A count of zero on the vitals is the difference between "green" and "working.".

    Worth building the same gap into the rollout rather than only into the checking. The first apply creates the checks without running them:.

    Create, inspect, then arm. Nothing is billed in between, and the review happens against real objects rather than a strategy diff.

    Because k6 reports web vitals in milliseconds, and the panels had been declared in seconds. Grafana rendered 613 ms as "613 s", compared it against thresholds meant for seconds, and painted the entire dashboard red while the sites were, in fact, fast.

    Industry observers note that the diagnosis is the exception. Cumulative Layout Shift is the one Core Web Vital with no unit — it's a ratio. It was the only panel still green.

    Everything red except the unitless metric is a unit bug, not an outage. That is a genuinely reusable tell, and it generalizes past this dashboard: when a fault hits every member of a set except the one that differs in exactly one property, that property is the fault. A real performance collapse has no reason to spare CLS; a seconds-versus-milliseconds error cannot touch it.

    What the numbers looked like once the units were right:.

    Recent findings suggest that comfortably inside the "good" band, LCP included, against a 2500 ms budget. The dashboard had been claiming a site-wide emergency.

    A page quietly leaving a script.

    Industry observers note that consider the shape of it: several sites share one check, so a check covers many URLs. If one URL stops being visited — an inventory edit, a template change, a goto that throws where the loop swallows it — then probe_success stays 1, every panel stays green, the alert rules have nothing to fire on, and that page is simply no longer measured. There is no red anywhere. The monitoring reports health for a page it isn't looking at.

    Nothing in the metrics catches that, because the absence of a series is not a series. So the count has to be compared against an expectation that lives outside the metrics — and Terraform already holds it, in the inventory:.

    Sources indicate that the expected number is baked in at generation time. Fewer URLs reporting than configured turns the tile red.

    With one deliberate exception that took a round to get right: this tile ignores the dashboard filters. Every other panel follows them. Filter the view down to two news checks and 15 URLs report — correct, healthy, and displayed as a failure, because the tile was comparing a filtered count against the full-estate threshold. The fix isn't to make the threshold follow the filter; it's to make the tile refuse the filter, because it answers a question about the whole estate rather than about the current view.

    That's the general rule worth taking: a panel comparing against a global expectation must not inherit a local filter. Mixing the two produces a monitor that goes red when someone narrows the view, which trains people to ignore it — the worst outcome available for an indicator whose entire job is to be believed.

    Three things that aren't bugs but will be reported as bugs.

    Check runtime next to page metrics. A check walking twelve pages takes about 25 seconds. Placed beside LCP and TTFB, that number reads as though a page took 25 seconds to load. It describes the check — roughly 2 seconds per page including a browser start each — so it belongs in a collapsed section at the bottom, with the other mechanics. The dashboard is otherwise ordered by the sequence in which questions actually get asked: is everything green, what stands out, then each page individually, then how the check itself behaved.

    Ad blockers break classic dashboards entirely. Not the custom one specifically — every classic dashboard, including the vendor's own. The per-check Synthetics pages keep working, because those are app pages rather than dashboards. The result is a failure that looks extremely specific to your configuration when it's precisely the opposite, and it will consume an afternoon before someone tries a different browser.

    Mobile is emulation, not a slow phone. The mobile check sets a 412×915 viewport at scale 2.625, touch, and an Android user agent. It changes viewport, user agent, and touch. It throttles neither CPU nor network. Those numbers describe the mobile layout over a datacenter connection, which is a useful thing to track and not the thing most people assume they're reading. Label it on the panel, or someone will quote it in a meeting as what customers experience.

    And one absence that's a design decision rather than a gap: there is no INP. Interaction to Next Paint requires a real interaction, and a test browser doesn't click. It isn't collectible synthetically at all — it belongs to real-user monitoring, and its absence from a lab dashboard is the boundary working as intended. An earlier post covers what INP does catch, in the place it can be caught.

    #10579. LLMON: An LLM-Native Markup Language, now in Granite 4.1 3B and 8B

    📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1612 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

    LLMON: An LLM-Native Markup Language, now in Granite 4.1 3B and 8B

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1612 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that LLMs rely on their context to generate the next set of tokens.
    • Industry observers note that to address this, we developed LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced “lemon”), an LLM-native markup language for explicitly communicating structure and semantics to the models.
    • Today we are releasing two experimental preview models, derived from Granite 4.1 base models, trained to consume and generate LLMON-marked text: granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that LLMs rely on their context to generate the next set of tokens. Over a long trajectory, the context fills with numerous types of components: a system prompt, past conversation turns, instructions that act on retrieved documents, tool responses or user data, requirements constraining the allowed output, and reasoning chains. The context carries a rich structure, most of which is either implicit to the model or encoded in formats such as JSON that were not designed to be digested by LLMs. This is one of the main reasons LLMs, particularly those on the smaller end of the scale, are brittle and sometimes fail in unexpected ways. The lack of explicit structure can also be exploited by attackers, for example, in the form of prompt injections.

    Industry observers note that to address this, we developed LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced “lemon”), an LLM-native markup language for explicitly communicating structure and semantics to the models. Semantically coherent components are marked with meaningful tags which are wrapped in reserved special-token delimiters. Data schemas, including nesting, are stated in a way that is unambiguous to a causal LLM. Unique IDs make it possible to point to specific instructions, which could reside anywhere in the context, and bind them to the data payloads they should act on, analogous to the way functions are called and arguments are passed to them in programming languages.

    Today we are releasing two experimental preview models, derived from Granite 4.1 base models, trained to consume and generate LLMON-marked text: granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview. We are also releasing a GitHub repo, which includes a toolkit for working with LLMON and examples of workflows and templates.

    JSON was designed for parsers, not for causal language models. The tokenizer is not constrained to respect the grammar, and structure is encoded by tokens ({, ", :) that may also appear in normal text. To a model, a quotation mark inside a document and a quotation mark that closes a field are the same token. Escaping rules that are clear to a parser are only statistical patterns to a model. Nesting depth is encoded by counting brackets, which transformers are known to be weak at, especially over long spans.

    It has been revealed that LLMON, on the other hand, is an XML-like markup whose structural delimiters are reserved special tokens rather than characters, so structure and content use separate parts of the vocabulary. Tags are stated at the beginning of each span, and the boundaries between spans are explicit. Nested structures are stated locally so the model does not need to keep track of the hierarchy over long spans.

    Since most teams already have pipelines built around JSON, we created conversion tools and example notebooks that translate JSON to LLMON and back in a lossless manner.

    It has been revealed that LLMON does not replace chat templates; rather, it enriches them. Where regular chat templates tell the model which part belongs to which role (system, user, assistant), LLMON tells it what each component means and how components relate to each other, within and across roles.

    The LLMON preview models ship with their own chat template, so you build the same messages list you would pass to any chat model and call apply_chat_template as usual; it renders the LLMON shown below. The only difference is that a turn can now name its parts and mark each one exec: True or False. A part marked True is bound into the exec block at the bottom of the rendered output, which states which instruction to run and what it operates on; a part marked False is still rendered into the context but is referenced by nothing.

    Which the model receives as the following (with newlines and indentation added here for readability, as the template emits none):.

    The two-character block IDs are drawn from a fixed set that this tokenizer encodes as single tokens, so addressing a block always costs two tokens regardless of which ID is drawn.

    It has been revealed that the role is still a single user turn, but its components reach the model as five separate addressable blocks, bound together by a sixth (the exec block) that states: run this instruction, on this data, subject to these two requirements, and put the answer in the block named here, which is the same assistant block the model then fills. A conventional template would have flattened all components into one string and left the model to infer which part was the task, which was the subject, and which were constraints.

    Industry observers note that indirect prompt injection is a type of attack where a malicious instruction is hidden in a data payload, such as a retrieved document, a tool response, or user-provided data. This is the problem LLMON’s instruction/data separation is designed to address.

    We compared the LLMON previews against several open-source and closed-source models. We evaluated on the OPI benchmark, which places the injection in the data of classic NLP tasks. Several attack strategies are employed. We report robustness, defined as 1 − attack success rate: the share of attacks where the model does not carry out the injected instruction.

    All non-LLMON models are highly susceptible, carrying out the injected instructions with high probability. LLMON practically eliminates the problem on this benchmark, avoiding 47% more attacks relative to the best frontier model that we tested, and 95% more than the best open-source model. We observe similar trends on other benchmarks (ASB and StruQ). It is worth noting that these benchmarks test robustness to static indirect prompt injections. The instruction/data separation directly addresses this type of attack. We are actively working on also improving adaptive attacks which unfold over many chat turns.

    Sources indicate that safety gains don’t come at the expense of general capability. Across standard benchmark categories, the LLMON models perform on par with the Granite 4.1 Instruct models.

    Industry observers note that in short, if you’re experimenting with Granite 4.1 3B or 8B today, you can swap in the LLMON preview and should see comparable general performance with much stronger resistance to prompt injection. No conversion pipeline is required. Naming the turn's parts (e.g., instruction, data, requirement as in the example above) is enough. The shipped chat template turns those into LLMON blocks for you. Our LLMON-converters library goes one level deeper: if a part is itself structured, such as a JSON document, LLMONizing it preserves that structure as typed, individually addressable blocks, instead of one opaque string.

    The models start from Granite 4.1 base checkpoints rather than the released instruct models, so LLMON behavior is learned during post-training rather than layered on an existing chat format.

    Industry observers note that LLMON defines six delimiters that mark the start and end of tags and allow nesting and anchoring; they are installed in the tokenizer as reserved single tokens. We re-serialized a conventional instruction-tuning corpus into LLMON: every prompt component becomes its own addressable block, and each turn carries an execution block naming which instruction to run, which inputs it operates on, and where the output goes. The task mix is the one a normal instruct model sees (chat, multi-turn, RAG, tool calling), which is why benchmark performance stays close to the conventionally tuned model. In addition, we augment the data with decoy instructions and data blocks that are present in context but deliberately left unbound, while the target output is unchanged. So the model learns to follow the dependencies dictated by the execution block and ignore the rest. Reinforcement learning follows: five sequential GRPO stages spanning multi-domain reasoning, RLHF, knowledge calibration, and math, followed by a final DPO stage on a thousand on-policy preference pairs built from the model’s own responses to injection attempts.

    The resulting privilege rule falls out of this layout rather than an added guardrail: an instruction reached through an execution block is authoritative, while anything reached as input (data, documents, tool schemas, tool results) is material to read, not a command to follow. Furthermore, instructions and data spans that are not called on in the execution block are ignored. This is a learned behavior, not an enforced guarantee. To see how this plays out in the attention layers of a LLMON model, try the LLMON Attention Visualization on Hugging Face Spaces.

    LLMON is not tied to a fixed schema: you can choose tag names and structure that fit your domain and fine-tune an adapter to read and write them. We demonstrate this on ScienceWorld, a text-based benchmark where an agent carries out elementary science tasks (such as boiling water) by issuing one command at a time and receiving a score from the simulator. We defined a vocabulary capturing the structure in the planning trajectories involved in solving these tasks. The vocabulary includes tags such as instr.task.goal, req.planning_policy.rule, data.state.room, data.state.inventory and assistant.next_action. We rendered every step of ScienceWorld's reference solutions with these tags and tuned a LoRA on top of a LLMON model. The trained model then plays held-out games and writes its next action in the new vocabulary. This notebook walks through the full workflow, from converting reference trajectories to playing the test games and scoring the adapter against the untrained base model. Another example for tool-calling agents can be found in this notebook.

    This is an experimental preview, ready for exploration and evaluation but not for production.

    Sources indicate that tell us what you find: what worked, what broke, and which use cases you’d like to see. Post it in GitHub Discussions.

    That's really awesome! With an Apple pkl community renderer, you could potentially write PKL and render LLMON. 🥒🍋.

    Any-to-pkl-community will convert json, yaml, toml to pkl, so just need the render part.

    GratefulAgents Starts on Loopback, and Exposure Should Follow the Deployment

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (493 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • GratefulAgents is a self-hosted control plane for running AI-agent workflows against repositories.
    • It has been revealed that zoomEye returned zero for app="GratefulAgents", zero for the product title, and zero for the HTTP body.
    • Sources indicate that loopback binding prevents a dashboard from accepting connections from another host.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    GratefulAgents is a self-hosted control plane for running AI-agent workflows against repositories. The controller reconciles platform and trigger resources, exposes a dashboard, and can receive GitHub webhooks. A local Kind deployment binds the dashboard to 127.0.0.1:8090 and prints a command to retrieve the generated administrator password.

    It has been revealed that zoomEye returned zero for app="GratefulAgents", zero for the product title, and zero for the HTTP body. The application query is selected and all three probes succeeded. The result is consistent with a product that starts as a local control plane, but it does not prove that every deployment remains on loopback or stays out of an index.

    Sources indicate that loopback binding prevents a dashboard from accepting connections from another host. It does not prevent a reverse proxy from publishing the application later. The deployment should record the intended interface, the proxy configuration, the authentication method, and the administrator recovery process.

    Recent findings suggest that the local setup uses a generated administrator password. That password should not remain the only recovery path. Store it in a secret manager, require an administrator login, and define how it is rotated. If an identity provider is added, map groups to roles and keep the recovery account under separate control.

    Industry observers note that the project's connection-secret documentation says dashboard access alone does not grant permission to use a stored integration credential. That distinction should appear in the authorization model. A user who can view a run may not need the GitHub token that the run uses. A user who can create a project should not automatically receive every provider key.

    According to recent reports, inventory repository tokens, GitHub App private keys, OAuth tokens, webhook secrets, Kubernetes credentials, and provider keys. Record which runtime and which project can use each one. Check the service account that releases the agent container and the permissions available to the repository checkout.

    Sources indicate that for a local deployment, verify that the dashboard is reachable only from loopback and that no proxy route publishes it. For a Kubernetes deployment, inspect the Service, Ingress or Gateway, NetworkPolicy, TLS configuration, authentication mode, and administrator password retrieval path.

    Industry observers note that the zero external count is not an all-clear. Use DNS and proxy inventory to find a dashboard that the search engine did not index. Then test unauthenticated access, an ordinary user role, and an expired session.

    It has been revealed that agent runs can read repositories, write patches, use network tools, and produce artifacts. Review the image, runtime profile, mounted files, network egress, and tool policy. A run should not inherit a broad human token when a scoped repository credential is enough.

    According to recent reports, if a dashboard or secret path was exposed, revoke provider keys, webhook secrets, and Kubernetes credentials, then review runs that used them. The useful evidence is the link between a project, a run, a credential, and the repository or model action.

    What is Blockchain: Everything You Need to Know (2022)

    📅 18 Apr 2022 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1050 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Blogspot

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information.
    • Sources indicate that it’s like your computer’s hard drive.
    • Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

    Sources indicate that it’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain.

    Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

    A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

    A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

    Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

    Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

    To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:.

    Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

    Blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many users and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

    And that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more quickly than ever.

    Even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

    Recent findings suggest that blockchain already being adopted by some major-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

    Sources indicate that although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

    Tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

    Blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

    Industry observers note that blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

    Sources indicate that have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

    Blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

    Instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

    Blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a company's product inventory.

    Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages.

    I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

    In a recent development, blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

    According to recent reports, yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of users constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

    Coinbase Global is at the moment the biggest blockchain company in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

    Blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

    Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency.

    Generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

    Blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain. Hope you like this article if you have any question let me know in the comments section.

    llama.cpp v1.0.0 : A stronger foundation for the local AI ecosystem

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (547 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that llama.cpp makes it possible to run multi-modal LLMs across a wide range of hardware - from consumer-grade local machines to high-end enterprise servers.
    • In a recent development, during the 3.5 years since its inception, the project has grown a lot and many downstream applications already depend on our work.
    • Recent findings suggest that today we release libraries v1.0.0, highlighting our responsibility to those developers.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that llama.cpp makes it possible to run multi-modal LLMs across a wide range of hardware - from consumer-grade local machines to high-end enterprise servers. Through quantization, optimized backends, and a portable C/C++ implementation, we make AI inference accessible at every level of the software stack. We believe this is the most lightweight, versatile and sensible platform for building cross-platform and private AI products.

    In a recent development, during the 3.5 years since its inception, the project has grown a lot and many downstream applications already depend on our work. We expect this trend to continue as local AI and privacy become increasingly important in our everyday lives. Every newly introduced integration means more developers depending on our library interfaces and therefore having a flexible but stable API is paramount.

    Recent findings suggest that today we release libraries v1.0.0, highlighting our responsibility to those developers. Moving forward, both llama.cpp and ggml will reflect API and ABI incompatibilities with major-version bumps. As adoption grows, we will be stricter about making those boundaries visible to downstream consumers.

    The following rules apply to all ggml-org projects using semantic versioning:.

    We are looking forward to expanding the ways in which ggml-org software is distributed and reaches developers and end-users. For more information about how to add ggml-org projects to your packaging and release pipelines, please check the following discussion.
