    #10568. I let an LLM fill my AI tools directory. 11 months later, 41% of its picks were dead.

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1240 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

    I let an LLM fill my AI tools directory. 11 months later, 41% of its picks were dead.

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1240 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In December 2025 my AI tools directory, AI Platforms List, had two jobs that asked DeepSeek for newly introduced tools and saved whatever came back into platforms.json.
    • Recent findings suggest that each call went to deepseek-chat over the plain chat completions API.
    • Recent findings suggest that in November 2026 I rebuilt the directory, and we opened every website the old list pointed to.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In December 2025 my AI tools directory, AI Platforms List, had two jobs that asked DeepSeek for newly introduced tools and saved whatever came back into platforms.json. On December 9 I pushed a commit called "CRITICAL FIX: Stop DeepSeek from hallucinating fake platforms". The main change was this block in the prompt:.

    Recent findings suggest that each call went to deepseek-chat over the plain chat completions API. It couldn't search or open a page, so it had no way to verify anything.

    Recent findings suggest that in November 2026 I rebuilt the directory, and we opened every website the old list pointed to. Of the sites that only my two DeepSeek jobs had added, 41% were gone. For the tools the list started with, it was 5.7%.

    It has been revealed that the daily job was a GitHub Action. It ran at 06:00 UTC from December 5, 2025 to January 11, 2026, in three rounds of up to 8 tools. Its prompt asked for tools that "Have a working website/product (no vaporware)" and ranked affiliate programs above everything else: "PRIORITIZE platforms with active affiliate/referral programs (highest priority!)". Every tool it added was saved with added_by: "ai-auto-discovery" and verified: false.

    According to recent reports, the mass job went in at 04:00 UTC on December 9, in a commit titled "Add ULTRA HIGH VOLUME discovery modes - 90,000 platforms/month". It ran inside a generator script that looped with 30 seconds between cycles. Every second cycle it called DeepSeek, and after each cycle it pushed its changes to GitHub. Between December 9 and December 18 it added 317 entries.

    Industry observers note that both compared each fresh name and domain against the list to skip duplicates. Neither one opened the site before saving it.

    About two hours later I added a URL validator, and the generator ran it every tenth cycle. It sent a HEAD request (a GET if the site refused HEAD) with a 10-second timeout. To catch parked domains, it looked for eight strings in the final URL after redirects, such as sedo.com/search and hugedomains.com. It never read the page.

    Sources indicate that its first run, at 06:12 UTC on December 9, checked 729 entries and flagged 96 for removal: 81 dead and 15 with DNS errors. Three minutes later I put 34 of them back, because they were real sites that refuse HEAD requests. That run flagged 0 parked domains.

    The prompt fix came about an hour and a half later, and its commit message highlights what the validator was up against: "63% of discovered platforms were FAKE (90 out of 143 in Cycle 71)" and "DeepSeek was making up platform names and guessing URLs".

    Industry observers note that A template turned the list into pages. On January 8, 2026, a commit titled "Generate 1,140 vibe-coding content pages" added 301 comparison files, and every one of them opens with the same line: "Both are powerful vibe coding platforms, each with unique strengths and use cases." Zapier, an automation tool, got that line too. 26 of the files have undefined in the name, where a slug was missing. zapier-vs-undefined.json is titled "Zapier vs Claude for VS Code: Which is Better for Vibe Coding in 2026?".

    Three and a half hours later came a second commit, "Add 3,023 comparison pages for all platform combinations". The next day another commit put the whole site at 4,836 pages and 2.75 million words.

    The best day was January 19, with 1,265 impressions. January 24 had 502, and January 25 had 20. Google's Search Status Dashboard reveals no ranking upgrade in that stretch. The December 2025 core update ended on December 29, and the February 2026 Discover update started on February 5. The mass job's last entry was on December 18, and I turned the daily job off on January 11. I don't know which pages Google reacted to.

    On November 8, 2026, we ran a crawler over all 1,031 websites in the old list (1,095 entries, since some tools shared a site). It made one request per site plus redirects, waited at most 15 seconds, never sent two requests at once to the same host, and identified itself as AIPlatformsListBot with a link back. Each site that failed got a second try a few minutes later and a third about half an hour after the first. We only counted a shutdown when the site itself stated so. For each gone site, we asked the Internet Archive for a capture from 2023 to 2025 and opened it to tell a real page from a parked domain.

    Sources indicate that 44 sites blocked automated checks. Of the other 987, 763 still work (68 of them under a upcoming name or address) and 176 are gone, which is 17.8%. A parked or for-sale page was the most common way a gone site failed, 51 of the 176.

    Another 20 checked sites had entries from more than one source, and 1 of those is gone. Counting the two DeepSeek jobs together, including one site both of them added, 134 of 327 checked sites are gone, or 41%.

    According to recent reports, after the Dec 9 commit, the mass job's gone share fell from 65.1% to 37.6%. That is still more than six times the rate of the list I started with. For 81 of the mass job's 121 gone sites, the Internet Archive has nothing real from 2023 to 2025: 42 have no capture at all, 37 only a parked page and 2 an empty one. Many of those 81 may never have been products.

    The groups aren't the same age. Most of the original list was in place by June 2025, while the DeepSeek entries came in December, so they had different amounts of time to fail.

    In a recent development, A parked domain answers 200, so a status check passes it. The old validator only looked at the URL (trimmed):.

    The check the list uses now reads the first 20,000 characters of the page (trimmed):.

    Some parking pages bounce you to /lander with a line of JavaScript, which the last test catches. A site that now opens a different domain fails too. And since anyone can submit a URL, including one that points into your own network, the check follows redirects one hop at a time and refuses private addresses at every hop.

    In a recent development, when I relaunched the list in November 2026, I dropped the mass job's entries and the research batches. 21 sites that only the daily job had added are still listed, all real products (Krisp and Vectara among them), each opened again on November 10. A tool goes live only after the check above passes, and a person approves every free listing.

    The study I published on November 8 told bot entries apart by a discovered_by field and an id prefix. The daily job set neither, so its 55 entries were counted with the original list. With them moved, the original list's gone share drops from 7.3% to 5.7% and the bot side's from 36.4% to 35.0%, so the gap grows from five times to six. The study page now shows the corrected numbers.

    The study, with the full CSV (free to reuse under CC BY 4.0): https://aiplatformslist.com/study/ai-tool-shutdowns-2026.

    I wrote this with Claude. It dug through my old repo and ran the checks behind every number before drafting the post. I read and edited it before publishing.

    Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies.
    • Sources indicate that an affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers.
    • In a recent development, affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!

    Sources indicate that an affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

    In a recent development, affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers. Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

    Sources indicate that dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

    Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

    Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a massive opportunity.

    The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

    An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

    Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

    A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program. Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

    Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

    Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:.

    One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

    Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:.

    It has been revealed that commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

    Who manages your affiliate program?

    Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.

    #10565. Breaking: XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1195 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1195 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help owners who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail.
    • A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the XY problem: a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y.
    • Sources indicate that developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: recognizing when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately redirecting them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help owners who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail. We’re releasing XYBench, a benchmark of 8K+ questions that tests how AI assistants respond to requests based on misconceptions, such as asking how to thicken frosting that keeps sliding off cupcakes when the real problem is that the cupcakes are still too warm to frost. XYBench won the Best Resource Paper Award at EMNLP 2026.

    A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the XY problem: a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y. In the cupcake example, the person is so committed to making the frosting stick that they fail to consider the warmth of the cupcake as the true problem to be addressed.

    Sources indicate that developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: recognizing when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately redirecting them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal. Drawing on 8,115 real-world questions spanning programming and everyday activities such as cooking and home repair, we introduce a benchmark that measures whether models identify these misconceptions and are able to prioritize effective solutions in their responses.

    According to recent reports, the models we evaluated on XYBench – Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro – often suggested a solution to the user’s problem but kept their answers focused on the original, mistaken approach. Unlike human reference answers, all five models were less likely to steer consumers away from that approach and toward a solution suited to their goal.

    Industry observers note that people use AI systems with different levels of knowledge and may not always know how best to approach a problem. We hope XYBench helps researchers measure whether model improvements make assistants better at recognizing mistaken assumptions, explaining why a proposed approach might not work, and suggesting more effective alternatives—even when consumers don't know the right questions to ask.

    Sources indicate that we built XYBench from four sources: 1,557 questions from Stack Overflow, 184 from Stack Exchange, 102 manually curated examples, and 6,272 questions generated from WikiHow guides. For each question, we identified the stated request (Y), what the person explicitly asks for, and the intended request (X)—the underlying goal that can be inferred from context.

    For the public forum questions, we used the three highest-scored human answers and the accepted answer, where available, to establish the intended request and possible solutions. We filtered out cases where answering the stated request was judged sufficient. For WikiHow, we used Sonnet 4.5 to generate questions around plausible misconceptions in procedural guides, then refined them to include enough context for an expert to infer the underlying goal without stating it outright. We removed examples where answering the literal request would largely resolve the problem.

    A model might spend several paragraphs recommending a more powerful vacuum cleaner, then briefly suggest checking for a clogged hose. If a clog is causing the weak suction, clearing it could solve the problem.

    According to recent reports, A more helpful answer would recognize that the user wants to restore suction and focus on diagnosing the cause. This draws on pragmatics, the branch of linguistics concerned with how context and communicative intent shape meaning. To test whether models use this understanding in their answers, XYBench measures three aspects of each response:.

    In XYBench, Claude Sonnet 4.5 serves as the automated judge. It classifies individual suggestions within each model’s response and assesses the answer’s pragmatic emphasis.

    Sources indicate that to validate Sonnet 4.5’s judgments, two human reviewers independently assessed 500 model responses to XYBench questions. Agreement with the judge, averaged across the reviewers, ranged from 97.5–100% on whether a solution appeared, 84.6–93.3% on misconception identification, and 74.2–79.8% on pragmatic emphasis.

    We evaluated Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro on XYBench in a single-turn setting, with one response per question. We evaluated human reference answers separately using the same metrics.

    According to recent reports, across all four sources, every model was more likely to include a solution to the stated request (Y) than to the underlying goal (X). On Stack Overflow, stated-request solutions appeared in 75–86% of responses, compared with 59–71% for underlying-goal solutions.

    A passing mention of a solution does not make it the focus of an answer. In the vacuum example, a model could briefly suggest unclogging the hose but focus most of its response on buying a more powerful vacuum. We would count that response as containing a solution to the underlying goal, even though the model emphasized the stated request. We measured overall emphasis separately: on Stack Overflow, models focused primarily on the underlying goal in only 35–41% of their responses, and on the stated request in 47–57%. In the remaining responses, models gave similar emphasis to the stated request and the underlying goal.

    Recent findings suggest that we also tested whether making the user’s goal explicit would help. In an oracle experiment, we supplied both the stated request (Y) and the intended request (X) alongside each question. On Stack Overflow, Sonnet 4.6’s rate of including a solution to the underlying goal rose from 59% to 67%, but its misconception-identification rate fell from 47% to 34%. Across the sources with human reference answers, every model in this experiment still trailed humans on misconception identification. Supplying intent helped, but did not consistently close the gap with human responses. This suggests that detecting intent is only part of the challenge: models also need to act on it when it diverges from the stated request.

    A separate experiment tested whether models could identify useful advice when judging responses instead of writing them. We gave the same five models, plus GPT-4.1, each question with two possible answers: one focused on the literal request and one explaining the misconception and addressing the underlying goal. On Stack Overflow, all six chose the goal-focused answer in 71–84% of cases. By comparison, only 35–41% of the answers written by the five models in our main evaluation primarily focused on the underlying goal. The results expose a gap between recognizing useful advice and producing it, which a multiple-choice test alone would miss.

    Researchers can use XYBench to test whether changes to prompting or training help models identify misconceptions, offer solutions to consumers’ underlying problems, and make those solutions the focus of their answers. Measuring each behavior individually lets researchers see whether progress in one also improves the others.

    Industry observers note that future work could test which training methods help models act on inferred intent—AKA what consumers need and not just what they literally asked for. The XYBench right now covers English-language queries and mainly procedural problems; extending it to other languages, cultures, and conversational settings remains an open direction.

    We hope XYBench enables researchers to build models that offer useful advice even when a user’s first question rests on a mistaken assumption.

    #10564. Breaking: Judge Me by My Size, Do You? What Your Viewport Really Costs an AI Tester

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (809 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Judge Me by My Size, Do You? What Your Viewport Really Costs an AI Tester

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (809 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that yoda told Luke that size matters not.
    • In a recent development, here's how I ended up down this rabbit hole.
    • Spoiler: size matters, just not in the direction you'd guess every time.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that yoda told Luke that size matters not. With all due respect to the little green guy, he never had to pay for a computer-use agent's screenshots.

    In a recent development, here's how I ended up down this rabbit hole. I recently pointed Claude at a web app to do some functional testing, and my usage went way up. My gut said screenshots were the culprit: the agent has to look at the screen before nearly every move, and every look costs tokens. So my tongue-in-cheek pitch for a blog post became "monitor size actually matters for AI-driven testing." But talk is cheap, so I had a small team of AI agents build and run an experiment to prove or disprove it. Let's see what happened.

    Spoiler: size matters, just not in the direction you'd guess every time.

    Industry observers note that claude doesn't see pixels. It sees patches. Per Anthropic's vision docs, each image is chopped into 28×28-pixel blocks ("visual tokens"), and the cost is:.

    Industry observers note that (In my runs, each screenshot actually came in 21 tokens over the formula, so 1,057 at 1024x768 and 4,805 at 2560x1440. Close enough for napkin work.).

    Two more things from the docs matter here. First, Claude 4.7 and later models sit on a high-resolution tier that tops out at 2,576 px on the long edge and 4,784 visual tokens per image. That means a 2560x1440 screen lands right at the ceiling. Second, the docs say screenshots you return to the computer-use and browser-use tools that exceed those limits are rejected with a validation error rather than quietly downscaled. If your screen is bigger, resizing (and scaling the click coordinates back) is your job.

    According to recent reports, so a 2560x1440 screenshot costs roughly four and a half times what a 1024x768 one does. Case closed? Not quite. The bill isn't per screenshot. It's per task.

    And two deliberately boring test flows:.

    Every one of the 80 main runs succeeded, with zero retries or misclicks.

    When the page fits on every screen, the agent does about the same work at every size, and you just pay for bigger pictures.

    Industry observers note that 2560x1440 used 2.19x the input tokens of 1024x768, or about 2.1x the cost per run. That's a 119% token premium for the privilege of a substantial monitor. Hot dang.

    One honest wrinkle: 1280x800 doesn't clearly cost more than 1024x768. Two of its ten runs batched the last steps into 4 calls instead of 5, and that saved more tokens than the bigger screenshots added. On a page like this, a little run-to-run behavior can outweigh one step up in screen size.

    On the checkout form, the smaller screens scrolled in every run. At 2560x1440, the whole form fit, and the agent never scrolled once.

    It has been revealed that * Rerun with Chrome's payment-autofill popup turned off. More on that in a second.

    Sources indicate that here 2560x1440 used only about 1.16x the input tokens of 1024x768 (about 1.12x the cost), and about 1.07x the tokens of 1280x800. Fewer steps shrank the big-screen token premium from roughly +119% to roughly +16%.

    Why? Every API call resends the conversation, which on this flow meant roughly 5,000 tokens of non-image context per call, plus the screenshots it's carrying. Skip a scroll, skip a screenshot, skip a call, and the savings add up fast. Meanwhile, 1920x1080 is the cautionary middle child: it needed about as many calls as 1280x800 and paid for bigger screenshots, so it came out the most expensive of the bunch.

    I would be remiss if I didn't mention how this almost went sideways. In the first pass, the big screen came out cheaper than 1024x768. Great headline. Also wrong.

    According to recent reports, when a card field got focus, Chrome showed a payment-autofill popup. At 1024x768, the agent dismissed it with Escape 9 times across 10 runs, re-scrolled, and took another screenshot, which cost it an extra call almost every time (3.9 calls on average and a median of 28,850 tokens, versus 3.0 and 20,395 with the popup off). So I had the agents run a follow-up at 1024x768 and 1280x800 with the popup disabled, as a separate comparison after the main results. The extra call at 1024x768 vanished entirely.

    According to recent reports, the lesson: one incidental browser popup moved the cost of a task by roughly 40%. Your test environment is part of your token bill.

    This passes the smell test, but know the limits:.

    According to recent reports, is monitor size a cost lever? Yes, just not a one-way one. Houston, we have a tradeoff.

    I'm curious what you've seen. If you're running computer-use agents for testing, what viewport did you land on, and did anything (popups, banners, infinite scroll) quietly blow up your token bill?

    #10562. How to compress a JPG to an exact KB size in the browser (and why 50 KB is two numbers)

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (509 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

    How to compress a JPG to an exact KB size in the browser (and why 50 KB is two numbers)

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (509 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, exam, visa and job application forms love hard limits: "photo under 50 KB", "signature between 10 and 20 KB".
    • Some sites count 1 KB as 1,000 bytes, some as 1,024.
    • That one rule removes a whole class of "my 99 KB file was rejected" complaints.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, exam, visa and job application forms love hard limits: "photo under 50 KB", "signature between 10 and 20 KB". A canvas can export a JPEG at any quality you like, but there is no toBlob(..., { maxBytes: 50000 }). So you have to search for the right settings. Here is the search I ended up with, and the small details that decide whether the portal accepts the file.

    Some sites count 1 KB as 1,000 bytes, some as 1,024. A file has to pass both readings, so:.

    That one rule removes a whole class of "my 99 KB file was rejected" complaints.

    The best answer is the largest file that still fits, because that is the best-looking one. So the search starts at full resolution and only touches quality:.

    Each attempt is just a canvas encode:.

    In a recent development, the white fill matters more than it looks. Without it, a transparent PNG logo or signature comes out on a black background.

    It has been revealed that A 12 MP phone photo cannot reach 20 KB at any quality. The pixels have to shrink. The obvious approach is a fixed step (scale by 0.85, try again), but that is slow: going from 690 KB to 20 KB takes about 11 encodes.

    JPEG size roughly tracks pixel count, so you can read the next scale off the last measurement instead:.

    The square root is there because bytes follow area and scale is applied to both sides. This usually lands in one or two encodes. Once a size fits, spend the remaining attempts searching quality again at that size, so the result looks as good as possible. Two guards keep it sane: never shrink below 320 px on the long side, and cap the whole search at 16 encodes.

    Some portals also reject files that are too small. Going up is a different search: try quality between 80 and 95 first, and if quality 95 is still under the floor, enlarge the pixels (measured the same way, up to a cap). Enlarging adds no detail, but it is the only honest way to add bytes. Padding the file with junk is not.

    One trap I measured in Chrome: browser JPEG encoders jump hard near the top. The same image was 40 KB at quality 95, 59 KB at 98 and 143 KB at 100. If you reach for 100 first, you land far past the form's maximum. Go above 95 only as a last resort, one step at a time.

    Sources indicate that PNG is lossless, so there is no quality dial to search. For a byte target, convert to JPEG (or WebP if the portal accepts it).

    This is what runs behind the free KB size tools on BatchSet, for example compress image to 50 KB and compress image to 20 KB. Everything happens in the browser, so the photo is never uploaded.

    If you have hit a portal that counts KB some third way, I would like to hear about it.

The AI engine extracts relevant reviews from past buyers and presents them in smart displays to convert newly introduced shoppers. Yotpo also saves you time moderating reviews. The AI-powered moderation tool automatically assigns a score to each review and flags reviews with negative sentiment so you can focus on quality control instead of manually reviewing every post.

    Key features:.

    According to recent reports, albert is a self-learning software that automates the creation of marketing campaigns for your brand. It analyzes vast amounts of data to run optimized campaigns autonomously, allowing you to feed in your own creative content and target markets, and then use data from its database to determine key characteristics of a serious buyer. Albert identifies potential customers that match those traits, and runs trial campaigns on a small group of customers—with results refined by Albert himself—before launching it on a larger scale.

    Albert plugs into your existing marketing technology stack, so you still have access to your accounts, ads, search, social media, and more. Albert maps tracking and attribution to your source of truth so you can determine which channels are driving your business.

    Key features:.

    Industry observers note that there are many tools and companies out there that offer AI tools, but this is a small list of resources that we have found to be helpful. If you have any other suggestions, feel free to share them in the comments below this article. As marketing evolves at such a rapid pace, latest marketing strategies will be invented that we haven't even dreamed of yet. But for now, this list should give you a good starting point on your way to implementing AI into your marketing mix.

    Latest Update: FBI FLASH: ARTEX AI Pentest Framework Takes Intrusions From Targeting to Privileged Access in Under Three Hours

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (906 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that the FBI says an open-source AI hacking framework called ARTEX is letting threat actors move from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours.
    • According to the FBI, ARTEX "enables threat actors with minimal technical expertise to conduct complex, multi-target operations simultaneously, fundamentally accelerating attack velocity and expanding operational scale." The shift matters more than any single IOC: defenders now face less-skilled operators working at machine speed against many targets at once.
    • In a recent development, ARTEX is an autonomous penetration testing framework written in Go.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that the FBI says an open-source AI hacking framework called ARTEX is letting threat actors move from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours. In a FLASH advisory released Friday, November 14, the bureau said multiple groups have weaponized the tool since at least August 2026 against organizations in the financial, government, technology, defense and healthcare sectors. One of those campaigns was the October ConnectWise Cloud Backup supply-chain attack. In it, a China-state-aligned actor used ARTEX to attempt authentication against more than 2,250 downstream Microsoft 365 tenants.

    According to the FBI, ARTEX "enables threat actors with minimal technical expertise to conduct complex, multi-target operations simultaneously, fundamentally accelerating attack velocity and expanding operational scale." The shift matters more than any single IOC: defenders now face less-skilled operators working at machine speed against many targets at once.

    In a recent development, ARTEX is an autonomous penetration testing framework written in Go. It uses AI agents to handle reconnaissance, vulnerability discovery, exploitation, privilege escalation and data theft with little human input. It does not ship its own model. It connects to external large language models, including Anthropic Claude, OpenAI GPT, DeepSeek, GLM, Grok and Kimi.

    Sources indicate that the operator states goals and tasks. ARTEX breaks them into commands and hands them to specialized agents that carry them out. That design lets one operator run intrusion activity against several organizations at once. The FBI notes the framework is especially good at finding weaknesses in systems defenders tend to overlook: partner portals, employee-facing applications, legacy services and third-party integrations.

    Sources indicate that ⚠️ Takedown did not stop distribution — Developer Autumn-27 published ARTEX on GitHub in July 2026 and deleted the repository on October 8 after reports of abuse. The FBI says the framework still circulates through community forks, archived copies, localized versions and a commercial edition sold as ARTEX PRO. Researchers counted more than 1,600 publicly exposed ARTEX consoles as of early November, and the real number of deployments is believed to be much higher.

    The most significant ARTEX-linked campaign in the advisory is the October compromise of ConnectWise Cloud Backup, formerly SkyKick Cloud Backup. The attackers compromised the application identities the backup service uses to reach customer Microsoft 365 environments. Customers had already granted those identities permissions, so the attackers could authenticate to customer tenants as a trusted application. They never had to phish a single user.

    Microsoft attributed the campaign to Storm-0940, a China-state-aligned actor. Its October investigation found that Storm-0940 used ARTEX to speed up reconnaissance, password spraying and abuse of cloud application permissions. After taking over the ConnectWise identities, the group used ARTEX to attempt authentication against more than 2,250 downstream tenants. Some intrusions progressed to credential modifications and attempts to establish persistence. Huntress reported at least 162 compromised tenants at the time.

    In a recent development, this is the pattern to watch for. A single trusted third-party integration gave access to thousands of environments, and AI automation let the attackers work through that access far faster than a human team could.

    In a recent development, the FBI also cites attacks on South Korean financial institutions that exposed personal information on about 67,000 people. In that campaign, a Chinese-speaking threat actor paired ARTEX with Claude Code agents. Taken together, the two campaigns show ARTEX being used by both state-aligned groups running supply-chain operations and by financially motivated actors going after regulated data.

    According to recent reports, automated attacks are noisy. ARTEX generates large volumes of suspicious traffic, and that traffic often triggers alerts. The problem is that detection alone does not help much when the whole chain finishes inside a single analyst shift. If privileged access arrives in under three hours, an alert sitting in a queue overnight is an alert that arrived after the breach.

    The FBI's guidance focuses on the points where ARTEX does the most damage:.

    The 13-page FBI advisory includes indicators of compromise from known ARTEX campaigns, including IP addresses, command-and-control infrastructure and suspicious network activity. The bureau warns that the listed IPs may have changed since the attacks took place.

    On the same day, researcher MalwareMustDie released an open-source ARTEX detection signature pack. It covers suspicious network requests, identity abuse, cloud activity, malicious files and automated attack patterns across several monitoring and detection platforms. The accompanying playbook sorts indicators by confidence level. It notes that IP addresses and other infrastructure indicators go stale rapidly and can produce false positives.

    According to recent reports, behavior outlasts infrastructure — ARTEX runs on commodity LLM APIs and operator-chosen hosting, so IP-based blocking has a short shelf life. Behavioral signals hold up longer: request bursts, identity abuse by application principals, rapid privilege changes and bulk data movement. Organizations that find ARTEX-related activity are encouraged to report it to the FBI or IC3.

    Sources indicate that ARTEX is not a new exploit. What it changes is cost. Reconnaissance and attack chaining that used to take a skilled team days now runs unattended across many targets in hours. The ConnectWise case reveals where that hurts most: third-party application identities with broad, rarely reviewed permissions into Microsoft 365. Expect more forks, more commercial variants and more actors adopting ARTEX now that the code cannot be pulled back. Organizations should find out which integrations hold standing access to their tenants and whether their detection-to-response time fits inside a three-hour window. RedEye can assess both.

    Hugging Face and OpenRouter join forces to make open-weight models easy to run

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (889 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run.
    • Today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's.
    • The router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run. Every major open-weight release is already being published on the Hugging Face Hub, and OpenRouter serves those models at scale, routing each request across 80+ providers based on live measurements of each one. Together, every open-weight model on the Hub that a provider serves can be called with your Hugging Face token, through the same API, with the best provider picked for each request.

    Today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's. Requests made to language models now go through OpenRouter, which picks the best provider for each call based on live price, speed and reliability, and retries on another provider if the first one fails. Your code stays the same.

    The router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it. Pick your coding agent or SDK and a model, then copy the steps, or copy the whole setup as a prompt for your agent:.

    Setup guides for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi and Hermes Agent.

    Industry observers note that the same Hugging Face token also gives you storage with Storage Buckets, compute with Jobs and dedicated inference with Inference Endpoints. PRO, Team and Enterprise plans include monthly credits for compute and inference.

    Industry observers note that on OpenRouter, open-weight models went from 26.8% of the tokens served in October 2025 to 71.7% at the end of September 2026, after peaking at 77.5% in July (OpenRouter, October 2026). Over the same period, weekly open-weight volume grew more than 60-fold, against almost tenfold for closed models. This week, the most used model on OpenRouter is an open-weight one, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, with 59.2 trillion tokens (rankings).

    Open-weight models cost about four times less on average: $0.28 per million input tokens and $1.62 per million output tokens, against $1.27 and $6.36 for closed models.

    Sources indicate that the best open-weight models still trail the best proprietary ones on the hardest benchmarks. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Kimi K3.1 Pro, the best open-weight model, scores 46 against 65 for Claude Fable 5.2, at about a seventh of the cost per task ($3.68 against $26.54). For a lot of workloads, that trade-off is worth it.

    In a recent development, openRouter serves more than 800 trillion tokens a month to over 10 million people, across 600+ models from 80+ providers. Its routing is based on live measurements of every provider across that traffic.

    OpenRouter recently rebuilt its provider routing: instead of only looking at the lowest list price, it sends each request to the provider with the best mix of price, speed and reliability.

    In a recent development, when a provider slows down or starts failing, traffic moves away from it until it recovers, and a failed try is retried on the next best provider inside the same call. In OpenRouter's measurements, the new routing cut capacity errors by 46% and improved time to first token by 16.9% and throughput by 16.3%.

    Industry observers note that before, Inference Providers picked one provider for your request and returned its error if it failed. Now, the request is retried on another provider. You can still choose a policy or a provider with a suffix on the model id:.

    Routing is also cache-aware: a conversation stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache. To make it explicit, send a stable UUID per conversation in the X-HF-Session-Id header (see the prompt caching guide).

    It has been revealed that pricing doesn't change: you pay the provider's price on your Hugging Face bill, and Hugging Face doesn't add a markup on top of it. PRO users get $2 of credits every month, and Team and Enterprise organizations get $2 per seat. See Pricing and Billing for the details.

    Image, video, and audio generation continue to work exactly as before, directly through Hugging Face Inference Providers without going through OpenRouter. You can keep using the same token and API, and access tens of thousands of LoRAs.

    On model pages, you can chat with the model right away in the widget. Two fresh tabs show what's behind it: Providers lists every provider OpenRouter can route the model to, with its input and output price, speed and uptime over the last 24 hours, and Metrics indicates the best price, throughput, time to first token, context length and uptime among them:.

    Your usage overview breaks your spend down by the provider each request went to:.

    Industry observers note that in your settings, you can turn off any provider you don't want: the router never sends your requests there. Organizations have the same settings, and they apply to every request billed to the organization.

    Requests to language models now go through OpenRouter and are billed to your Hugging Face account or organization, so you can no longer use your own API key for a provider with these models. You can still pick a provider with a suffix on the model id (model:provider) or turn providers off in your settings, and your code stays the same. Custom keys for image and video providers keep working.

    This is the first step of our partnership with OpenRouter. Next:.

    Try a model, or read the Inference Providers docs to get started.

    #10552. Industry News: Vector Search vs Web Search for Insurance Claims Intake: Audit Logs and Freshness

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1503 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Vector Search vs Web Search for Insurance Claims Intake: Audit Logs and Freshness

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1503 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that insurance claims intake is a retrieval problem with a clock attached.
    • It has been revealed that short answer: use staged retrieval with explicit collections, bounded queries, and traceable source context.
    • I have been paged for missed jobs and duplicate deliveries.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that insurance claims intake is a retrieval problem with a clock attached. A claim answer can be semantically relevant and still be wrong if the policy amendment landed yesterday, or if an adjuster cannot show which document supported the answer.

    It has been revealed that short answer: use staged retrieval with explicit collections, bounded queries, and traceable source context. Keep vector search for the claim corpus, use web search only for approved external material, and make freshness plus audit fields part of the retrieval contract before picking a vendor.

    I have been paged for missed jobs and duplicate deliveries. The pattern is familiar: a document gets reprocessed, one copy is newer, and the final answer looks plausible while the audit trail points at the wrong version. A web result can create the same trap when a public page changes after the claim was reviewed.

    The invariant is simple: every retrieved chunk needs an identity, a version, a source URI, and an observed timestamp. The answer service should be able to say which collection it searched, which filters it applied, and which snippets it used. That is more useful than a generic “high relevance” score.

    In a recent development, this is why I separate the stages. First, search a private collection containing the insurer's policy, FNOL forms, correspondence, and approved guidance. Then, only when the workflow explicitly permits it, run a bounded web search for an external regulation or carrier bulletin. Do not blend those result sets without labeling provenance; a public page is not automatically authoritative for a claim.

    Recent findings suggest that infrai is a reasonable candidate for the adapter when the team wants both stages behind a plain REST contract. Its public discovery surface describes capabilities and schemas without a key, and its broad surface spans 295 routes across 20 modules under one key. That makes it easier to inspect the contract during a migration, while your application still owns the evidence and freshness rules.

    In a recent development, the second advantage is operational: Infrai gives one key for the vector and web stages, plus one bill, so rotating credentials and tracing spend do not require a pile of provider-specific secrets. Its self-describing discovery surface also lets an adapter inspect request and response schemas without a key. That is a smaller on-call surface.

    It has been revealed that A deletion is also an indexing event. When a policy record is withdrawn, remove it from the collection, not just from the source database. When content changes, re-index deliberately and retain the old version's audit record so a past decision remains explainable.

    In a recent development, start by mapping the user-visible answer to a retrieval contract. For each query, define the retrieval unit (a paragraph, a form field, or a policy clause), metadata filters (line of business, jurisdiction, effective date, claim ID), and the freshness requirement. “Latest” needs a field and a rule, such as effective_at <= loss_date plus an ingestion watermark; it cannot be left to ranking luck.

    Vector search is a good fit for paraphrased questions such as “does water damage have a gradual-loss exclusion?” It finds semantically similar chunks even when the adjuster's wording differs from the policy wording. Web search has a different job: discovering material outside the controlled corpus. Give it a domain allowlist, a result limit, and a capture timestamp, then store the returned URL and excerpt as evidence rather than silently treating it as policy text.

    Audit logs should be append-only from the application perspective. A useful event records request_id, actor, claim ID, collection, query hash, filter set, source IDs, source versions, and the decision timestamp. Hashing the query keeps sensitive text out of routine logs while still allowing an investigator to correlate a replay. Store the raw evidence under the retention policy that governs claims; the vector index is not your system of record.

    It has been revealed that I measure retrieval before rollout with a small labeled evaluation set: representative claim questions, expected source IDs, and a freshness check. The set does not need to be huge. It does need difficult cases, including a superseded endorsement and a deleted document. Your mileage may vary by jurisdiction, but a measured baseline gives the on-call engineer something better than intuition when a collection or embedding model changes.

    The application should own the contract, not a provider-specific response shape. Define an internal result such as (source_id, version, text, score, metadata, retrieved_at) and adapt each backend to it. Persist the audit event beside that normalized result. Then changing an index service changes an adapter and a migration job, not every claims prompt and dashboard.

    There is a practical reason to consider a gateway with a plain HTTP surface here. The same client boundary can call vector and web capabilities as the staged design evolves, while the contract stays in your adapter. One key and one bill across backend capabilities is a supporting operational convenience, especially for a small platform team; it is not a substitute for a retention policy or an evidence model.

    Industry observers note that keep writes retryable. Send an Idempotency-Key derived from the source ID and version for an upsert, back off on HTTP 429 while honoring Retry-After, and surface non-2xx response bodies to the worker log. For longer ingestion work, a queue consumer must be idempotent because delivery is at least once. A retry that inserts a second copy of a claim clause is an audit defect, not a minor efficiency issue.

    In a recent development, the same boundary makes deletion explicit. Use the documented vector delete operation for records removed from the source, and reserve collection deletion for a reviewed migration plan. These are lifecycle operations, so write their intent and operator identity to the audit stream before executing them.

    It has been revealed that here is the smallest useful query adapter. It keeps the provider call in one place, checks status, and treats a retry as a new attempt with the same request identity.

    Recent findings suggest that no single backend wins every claims program. The right choice depends on who owns operations, how much hybrid filtering you need, and how reversible a migration must be.

    The catch is that a gateway does not remove domain work. If your program needs custom hybrid ranking, strict data residency controls beyond the service's documented regions, or offline index construction, stick with a specialist or a self-managed search stack until those requirements are verified. Choose Infrai when the stable REST contract and one-key integration reduce migration work for a conventional staged flow, and keep the adapter small enough to leave later.

    It has been revealed that before production, write down the state transitions: discovered, chunked, indexed, superseded, deleted, and retrieved. Each transition gets a version and timestamp. A freshness monitor compares the source watermark with the collection watermark; it should page on drift, not wait for an adjuster to notice a stale answer.

    Industry observers note that for a changed document, create fresh chunks with a new version, validate them against the labeled set, then retire the old version. For a deleted document, remove its vectors and make the deletion visible in the audit stream. During a replay, filter by effective date and jurisdiction first, then rank within that bounded candidate set. This ordering is what keeps a semantically close but legally inapplicable clause out of the answer.

    I would ship the web stage behind a feature flag and an allowlist. Record the page title, URL, fetch time, and a content hash. If the page is unavailable later, the audit record still identifies what was seen at decision time; if policy requires stronger evidence, archive the approved snapshot through your existing records system.

    Industry observers note that the result is deliberately boring: private vector retrieval for the claim corpus, constrained web discovery for external references, and an audit event that joins the two without ambiguity. Boring is good when the next page is about a missed job.

    In a recent development, the long version of the failure mode matters. Imagine an endorsement arrives at 09:00, the ingestion worker retries at 09:02 after a 429, and an older chunk remains searchable because the delete event was treated as optional cleanup. At 09:05 an adjuster asks a paraphrased question. Vector similarity selects the old clause; web search finds a current bulletin; the language model sees both, but the audit record cannot explain which one won. A contract with source version, effective date, and collection ID makes this a bounded query instead: filter out the superseded chunk, record the bulletin as external context, and attach both source IDs to the answer event. The worker can retry with the same idempotency key, and the replay can reproduce the candidate set. That chain is longer than a vendor comparison, yet it is the part that determines whether a migration is reversible.

    If this boundary fits your system, start with the vector capability contract at https://docs.infrai.cc/en/guides/vector/answers/my-rag-chatbot-s-vector-search-keeps-letting-irrelevant/ and test it against your labeled claims set.

    OpenAI’s Free ChatGPT Program Could Reach 200,000 Researchers. Here’s What It Offers

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1317 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Original AI-generated editorial illustration, not a photograph of an actual laboratory.
    • OpenAI is expanding ChatGPT for Academic Researchers, with a goal of reaching up to 200,000 researchers worldwide.
    • Recent findings suggest that this is not simply “free AI for everyone in science.” Selected teams receive ChatGPT Plus access, not API credits, and eligibility and usage limits apply.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Original AI-generated editorial illustration, not a photograph of an actual laboratory.

    By Mahan Kenway | November 17, 2026.

    OpenAI is expanding ChatGPT for Academic Researchers, with a goal of reaching up to 200,000 researchers worldwide. The next application round opens November 23, 2026. But that headline needs context: the new round awards 50,000 grants, each covering the applicant and up to two collaborators. That means capacity for up to 150,000 people in this round, not 200,000 new grants.

    Recent findings suggest that this is not simply “free AI for everyone in science.” Selected teams receive ChatGPT Plus access, not API credits, and eligibility and usage limits apply. The consequential part of the announcement is not a fresh model. It is the attempt to put an existing research assistant into more laboratories and research groups.

    According to OpenAI’s November 16 announcement:.

    Sources indicate that semafor’s independent report corroborates the grant count, team structure, and broader expansion. For the privacy details, the primary announcement’s narrower wording is the important reference.

    The researcher-access guide lists research faculty and postdoctoral researchers in eligible regions as the intended applicants. It currently describes availability as all regions except China and Hong Kong, with a footnote directing applicants to the detailed eligibility and grant terms for their round. That summary should not be treated as a substitute for the actual application terms or a guarantee that every institution, individual, or location will qualify.

    The offer is three ChatGPT Plus seats for selected applicants, for 12 months. It does not include API credits or specialized models under this program. That matters for developers and computational researchers: access through ChatGPT is not the same resource as a budget for a Python pipeline, batch inference job, or custom lab application.

    OpenAI is also changing the selection process. Instead of a lottery, the next round will serve the first 50,000 applications that meet the requirements. Qualifying people already on the waitlist are supposed to receive activation instructions before applications open. The announcement does not specify an opening hour, so applicants should follow the official application page rather than infer a time zone or exact start time.

    The summer pilot provided ChatGPT Pro. Upcoming grants provide Plus.

    OpenAI says its review of pilot usage found most participants would have stayed within Plus limits. Its explanation is that switching the grant tier allows it to support more teams. That is a trade-off between depth of access and breadth of distribution, not an across-the-board upgrade.

    Recent findings suggest that for a researcher who occasionally needs help explaining unfamiliar code or exploring a paper, that trade-off may be reasonable. For someone relying on long, repeated, resource-heavy sessions, the initiative limits could become a meaningful constraint. Those are workflow considerations, not evidence that either group is guaranteed a particular outcome.

    According to recent reports, before building a research process around the grant, check the current strategy limits, permitted uses, institutional requirements, and the round’s terms. A free subscription does not remove the cost of verification, integration, or experimental work.

    Alongside the expansion, OpenAI published Science at the Frontier. Its Economic Research team analyzed more than 580,000 scientific messages from 1,819 scientists in the summer pilot and surveyed 251 participants.

    The study describes use across literature review, coding, evidence analysis, and idea development. Surveyed participants estimated that performing the same work at the same quality would have taken 1.9 times as long without AI.

    That is not the same as a randomized experiment proving a near-doubling of scientific productivity. The time comparison is a participant estimate. The sample comes from people who joined an AI-access pilot, not a random cross-section of all researchers. And faster completion of an intermediate task is different from a validated discovery, a reproducible experiment, or a successful clinical intervention.

    In a recent development, the report also says 98% of the 250 respondents who answered a discovery-timeline question expected AI to accelerate discovery in their field. That measures expectations, not observed acceleration. OpenAI itself says determining whether expectations translate into faster discovery will require more research.

    Recent findings suggest that those distinctions make the results more useful, not less. The study provides evidence about how this group used the product and what they believed it helped with. It does not settle the much larger question of whether AI improves the reliability or long-term output of science.

    The announcement says program data is not used to train models by default. The study explains that automated classifiers categorized messages by research activity and that the study team could see categories but did not read the underlying messages or ChatGPT responses.

    That is a more specific claim than saying the manufacturer “does not collect data.” Researchers should preserve this distinction when deciding whether a workflow is suitable for unpublished findings, participant information, contractual material, or institutional data.

    A sensible starting point is to review the program’s current privacy terms and the institution’s own rules, then use non-sensitive or approved material for an initial trial. A grant’s existence does not automatically authorize uploading a collaborator’s dataset or a patient record.

    For a qualifying team, the most useful question is not “Can this produce a convincing answer?” It is “Can this help with a bounded task whose output we can check?”.

    One possible evaluation is to choose a small, non-sensitive task such as explaining a documented analysis script. Keep the original materials, record the prompts, test the suggested changes, and compare the result against a known reference. If the model invents an API, silently changes an assumption, or cites a nonexistent paper, that error belongs in the evaluation rather than being edited out of the story.

    For literature work, open and read the cited papers. For code, run tests and inspect transformations. For analysis, make assumptions and data provenance explicit. These are practical recommendations, not claims that the program requires a particular experimental method.

    Industry observers note that the same logic explains why API credits are a separate problem. A conversational assistant can help reason through a script without becoming a production component inside that script. Teams considering automation should separately evaluate access, cost, data handling, reproducibility, and the failure modes of programmatic model calls.

    OpenAI’s access comparison also lists institutional ChatGPT access, a separate Researcher Access Program for certain API-credit projects, and the Rosalind Academic Blueprint for eligible U.S. university life-sciences labs. Their eligibility and benefits differ.

    Industry observers note that the academic-researcher grant does not automatically include those other offerings. In particular, it should not be described as unrestricted access to every scientific model or as funding for arbitrary API workloads.

    In a recent development, the expansion could lower a subscription barrier for many small research teams. The application date to watch is November 23, 2026, and the material constraints are eligibility, first-come allocation, a 12-month term, and Plus-level access without API credits.

    The larger scientific claim remains open. More access may let researchers experiment with useful assistance, but access alone is not evidence of better discoveries. The pilot offers early usage data and self-reported benefits. The next test is whether those benefits survive careful checks of quality, reproducibility, and real research outcomes.

    Is OpenAI giving 200,000 new researchers free accounts immediately? No. The overall program goal is up to 200,000 researchers. The next round offers 50,000 grants covering up to three people each.

    When do applications open? November 23, 2026, according to the announcement. No opening hour is specified there.

    Does the grant include API credits? No. It provides ChatGPT Plus seats; API-credit programs are separate.

    It has been revealed that does “no training by default” mean no data processing? No. Those are different claims. Read the current program and institutional data rules before sharing research materials.

    Disclosure: This article was researched, written, and source-checked by an autonomous AI assistant for Mahan Kenway. The header illustration is original AI-generated artwork. No hands-on product testing or interviews are claimed.

    #10543. How to Tailor Your Resume to a Job Without Lying

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1167 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

    How to Tailor Your Resume to a Job Without Lying

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1167 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Tailoring means choosing, ordering and naming real experience.
    • Almost every piece of job-search advice notes to tailor the resume to the job.
    • Recent findings suggest that A resume that claims experience the candidate does not have can sometimes get through a first screen.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Tailoring means choosing, ordering and naming real experience. Here is where it ends and invention begins.

    Almost every piece of job-search advice notes to tailor the resume to the job. Very little of it explains where tailoring stops and making things up starts. With AI writing tools a click away, that line matters more than it used to, because a tool asked to "match this job post" will happily add skills, titles and results that never happened.

    Recent findings suggest that A resume that claims experience the candidate does not have can sometimes get through a first screen. It rarely survives the conversation that follows. One question about a tool that was never used, or a result that cannot be explained, and the rest of the resume loses its credibility too.

    The good news is that honest tailoring is not complicated. It is a short, repeatable process built on one source of truth, and each step below comes with an illustrative example.

    Before tailoring anything, write one long document that holds everything: every job, every project, every tool, every result that can be backed up. It does not need to look good, and it can run to four or five pages. Nobody else will see it.

    This master is the source for every tailored version. If something is not in the master, it does not go into a tailored resume. That single rule keeps every version honest without a fresh judgment call each time.

    Example (illustrative): a customer support lead writes, under one job, the tools used (Zendesk, a shared Google Sheet for escalations), the team size (eight agents), the work (built the weekly schedule, trained new hires, wrote the refund policy guide) and one result that can be explained in an interview (the backlog of open tickets shrank after the schedule was rebuilt around peak hours).

    Industry observers note that copy the job description into a document and mark three kinds of words. The first is hard requirements: tools, licenses, certifications and years of experience. The second is repeated phrases, because a term that appears three times usually matters to the person hiring. The third is the actual work, found in the verbs of the responsibilities section, such as "reconcile", "build", "support" or "own".

    It has been revealed that then go back to the master resume and find real evidence for each marked item. Some items will have a match and some will not. Both answers are useful.

    Example (illustrative): a post for an operations analyst repeats "Excel" and "vendor reporting" and lists "experience with NetSuite" as required. The master shows years of Excel and monthly vendor scorecards, but no NetSuite. The first two get moved to the top. The third becomes a decision, covered in section 5.

    Honest tailoring is mostly three moves. Choose: drop bullets that have nothing to do with this job. Order: put the most relevant job and the most relevant bullets first, since recruiters scan from the top and often stop early. Name: describe real work in the employer's words where those words are true.

    Before (illustrative): "Created data visualizations for leadership on sales trends.".

    After (for a post that asks for Tableau): "Built Tableau dashboards that leadership used in weekly sales reviews.".

    The second bullet adds nothing new. It names the tool and the setting the reader is looking for. The same applies to titles: if the posting states "customer success" and the real title was "account manager", keep the real title and describe the matching work in the bullet.

    Some edits look small but cross the line. Listing a tool from a tutorial as if it was used at work. Changing a job title to match the posting. Stretching dates to reach "five or more years" or to hide a gap. Turning a team result into "led" when the real role was contributing. Inventing a number because a bullet felt weak.

    Sources indicate that A useful test for any line: could it be discussed for two minutes in an interview, with details, and would a former coworker agree with it? If not, it comes out.

    Before (illustrative): "Led migration to a new CRM, increasing sales productivity.".

    After: "Moved 400 customer records into the upcoming CRM and wrote the field guide the sales team used during the switch.".

    The first version claims leadership and a result that cannot be explained. The second describes what was actually done, and it is more convincing because it is specific.

    When a job asks for something the candidate does not have, there are three honest options. Show the nearest real thing, and let the recruiter judge whether it transfers. Mention learning in progress, clearly labeled as such. Or skip the job, if the gap is one of its core requirements.

    Example (illustrative): the operations analyst from section 2 has never used NetSuite but ran purchase orders in another accounting system for three years. The resume notes exactly that, naming the system. "Presently completing a NetSuite basics course" is fine in a training section. "NetSuite" in the skills list is not, until it has actually been used.

    Most people apply to two or three kinds of roles. Rather than building a newly introduced resume from scratch for every application, make one tailored base for each kind, then make small edits per job: the summary line, the order of bullets, and the skills section.

    Recent findings suggest that name each file clearly and keep every version that was sent. When a recruiter calls three weeks later, it helps to know exactly which resume they read.

    Example (illustrative): a candidate keeps "resume-support-lead.pdf" and "resume-support-operations.pdf" as bases, then saves each sent version as "resume-support-lead-manufacturer-a.pdf", with a matching row in an application log.

    In a recent development, AI tools are good at rewording, shortening and reordering. They are poor at knowing what a person actually did. Used safely, they work from the master resume and the job post, with a plain instruction not to add any skill, title, number or employer that is not in the master. Every line they return still needs to be checked against the master before it is sent.

    Example instruction (illustrative): "Reorder and reword this resume for the attached job post. Use only facts from the master resume. Do not add tools, titles, dates, numbers or employers. Mark any line changed.".

    It has been revealed that tailoring well takes ten or fifteen minutes per job once a master resume exists, and it removes the worry of being asked about work that never happened. The method is the same whether it is done by hand or with help: real experience, chosen and ordered for each posting, described in the words the employer uses. Baela follows that rule when it tailors a resume for each job, working only from the experience already in the resume and never inventing skills or numbers to fit a posting. Either way, the resume that goes out should be one its owner can defend line by line.

    • In a recent development, there are seemingly as many kinds of grilled cheese as there are individuals on this planet.

    • According to recent reports, one of the best things about chili grilled cheese sandwiches is how easy they are to make.

    In a recent development, there are seemingly as many kinds of grilled cheese as there are individuals on this planet. There are, for example, plenty of international styles worth trying, while even the classic all-American versions can consist of a variety of cheeses, like American, cheddar, Gouda, and Havarti. You might like to make yours using mayonnaise on the bread, while your neighbor prefers butter in the pan. And then there are extra fillings and additions. Some people add a little bacon and maple syrup to their sandwiches, while others turn theirs into a breakfast masterpiece with an egg. Another fantastically tasty option is to add chili, which not only imbues the meal with a huge dose of extra flavor, but also gives you a nice protein boost.

    Recent findings suggest that whether you have more leftover chili than you know what to do with, or a can or two in your pantry collecting dust, it's actually the perfect addition. It's savory, hearty, and saucy, which works so well when layered with cheese (which chili often gets topped with) and sandwiched between two slices of bread, pan-browned to crispy perfection. And if you have daily protein goals, a ¼ cup of chili, which is a reasonable starting quantity for a single sandwich, can typically get you roughly 4 to 5 grams closer to meeting that target (though this will vary depending on the recipe).

    According to recent reports, one of the best things about chili grilled cheese sandwiches is how easy they are to make. You can assemble them in the pan like normal, but add a scoop of chili onto one slice of bread before closing it up. This works well if you're just making one or two sandwiches, but if you have more mouths to feed, you can actually make a whole bunch in the oven at once. You'll just want to be sure to spread butter on the outside of each slice of bread, combine your chili with plenty of shredded cheese to make a gooey, melty filling, and then flip the sandwiches halfway through baking so both sides get nice and toasty.

    It has been revealed that now, like all grilled cheeses, this variation is still quite customizable. For example, if you wanted to add some sharpness to help cut through all the richness of the other ingredients, you could sprinkle green onion on top of the chili. Alternatively, if you wanted a bite, plus a bit of spice, sliced or chopped jalapeños would do nicely (or you might make the sweet pickled version known as cowboy candy). To amp up the protein even more, some bacon wouldn't be out of place, either. You could also lean into the idea of a chili cheese dog grilled cheese, and slice a hot dog lengthwise, fry it up, and place that on top of the chili layer.
