    #10531. Skip Butter And Milk: The Canned Ingredient That Makes Burgers Juicier

    📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (516 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foodrepublic ↗ Open Full Page

    Skip Butter And Milk: The Canned Ingredient That Makes Burgers Juicier

    📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (516 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foodrepublic

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Juicy burger patties are all about nailing the perfect ratio of fat, moisture, and protein for something that isn't wet or greasy but also isn't dry and crumbly.
    • Recent findings suggest that cream of mushroom soup may be billed as a shelf-stable meal in its own right, but the condensed version is a canned soup hack for many recipes thanks to its texture and flavor.
    • It has been revealed that chopped mushrooms for extra-juicy burgers is an increasingly common tactic, but evenly mixing all the little bits without overworking the meat is challenging.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Juicy burger patties are all about nailing the perfect ratio of fat, moisture, and protein for something that isn't wet or greasy but also isn't dry and crumbly. While butter and milk can certainly help, condensed cream of mushroom soup is a far better and easier alternative that perfectly strikes the balance when you use the right amount.

    Recent findings suggest that cream of mushroom soup may be billed as a shelf-stable meal in its own right, but the condensed version is a canned soup hack for many recipes thanks to its texture and flavor. It's had much of its moisture removed and therefore has a higher ratio of fat. While wet enough to infuse proteins with a bit of juiciness, its fat content helps preserve the tenderness and protect the existing moisture, all with the delicious umami of mushrooms. Condensed varieties also tend to be more potent, so the small amount you'll use for juiciness translates into a subdued but still noticeable taste.

    It has been revealed that chopped mushrooms for extra-juicy burgers is an increasingly common tactic, but evenly mixing all the little bits without overworking the meat is challenging. While wet ingredients are far easier to thoroughly disperse, they come with a caveat. You need a starch to hold and release the moisture unless you want it to drip out right away. Breadcrumbs are a common choice in meatballs and other ground beef recipes, and a ratio of half a cup of starch to one 10.5-ounce can to one pound of protein gets the job done quite well.

    In a recent development, burger patties made with condensed cream of mushroom soup are pretty forgiving and more difficult to dry out, but that doesn't mean you can just chuck them on the grill willy-nilly. To preserve the juiciness and keep them easy to work with, you need to know when to leave them alone, whether that's while they're raw, cooking, or resting.

    Immediately cooking a burger infused with condensed cream of mushroom soup leaves a lot of surface moisture. This ends up steaming it, so it doesn't develop a good crust and robs it of much of the juice you were attempting to preserve. Letting any patty chill in the fridge helps it firm up and makes it easier to manipulate on the grill, but it also allows the breadcrumbs to absorb the moisture to release later. Similar to marinating, it also helps to let the flavors mix a bit, so you don't end up with pockets of intense mushroom-ness that can ruin an otherwise good bite.

    According to recent reports, while exact timing varies based on your method, the 5-6-7 rule when cooking burgers is a reliable starting point. Five minutes on one side, six on the other, then seven minutes resting helps you balance enough heat to create a crust with enough time to ensure that the insides are not still raw. The resting is particularly important, as you don't want to release all your juice onto your plate or as steam and make your subsequent bites drier.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that when you want to upgrade your peanut butter and jelly sandwich, you don't have to splurge on high-priced bread or get particular about the jam like Ina Garten. How you prepare it can make all the difference, and treating it like a grilled cheese with a bit of butter on the outside can give you a serious result with even more serious flavor.

    In a recent development, toasting the exterior of your sandwich with butter in a pan gives you a golden-brown outside packed with richness and flavor. It brings out the best in your bread and warms the peanut butter and jelly for something as gooey as melted cheese but infinitely creamier. This is especially true if you use a top-ranked store-bought butter brand, since even a small amount acts like a seasoning and truly upgrades the whole thing. The toasted bread and melted insides create a dichotomy of textures that transforms one of the simplest recipes in the world into something more decadent and complex.

    While the heat won't caramelize the sugars in the jelly or toast the peanut butter fats, it does make them taste more delicious. Smell is just as vital as taste when enjoying a meal, and heat releases those aromas so you can enjoy them more. This is especially nice if you work with higher-end, complex ingredients like artisan jellies, as it lets you better experience each little nuance.

    A new preparation method means new opportunities for better flavor. While simple toasting alone is enough to make any mixture of ingredients delicious, taking inspiration from other recipes and choosing the right type of bread maximizes that effect.

    In a recent development, while you should avoid crusty bread for a PB&J because it tends to be a bit dry, this trick is a great way of getting around that. Even older bread gets a texture boost, transforming it from stale and brittle to crispy and delicious. If you're focusing on the rich, buttery flavor, using something full of dips and ridges, like sourdough or a rustic country-style loaf, only lets you use more butter for a thoroughly flavored exterior. Just be sure not to use something with deep holes that your filling can leak through, as it may burn in the pan and foul the flavor.

    If you want to take things even further, you can make the most decadent PB&J French toast with this method. It's especially great if you dip a soft, fluffy white bread or brioche in the egg mixture, giving you something that's pillowy on the inside and crispy on the outside. Butter alone can toast the bread, but the addition of milk and eggs adds binding proteins and delicious fats that create a stronger, but still crispy, structure that holds its shape well and prevents the liquidy insides from oversaturating the bread.

    #10525. This Chain Was Dunkin's Bitter Rival In The '50s — Now It's The Most Popular Donut Spot In Japan

    📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (599 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foodrepublic ↗ Open Full Page

    This Chain Was Dunkin's Bitter Rival In The '50s — Now It's The Most Popular Donut Spot In Japan

    📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (599 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foodrepublic

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, dunkin' is one of America's favorite spots to grab a quick donut and one of its famous syrup-infused iced coffees — which we ranked from worst to best.
    • What makes this feud particularly fascinating is that it was a family affair.
    • As is often the case, feuds rarely end with a clear winner.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, dunkin' is one of America's favorite spots to grab a quick donut and one of its famous syrup-infused iced coffees — which we ranked from worst to best. Today, the chain boasts more than 10,000 stores in the U.S. alone and sits comfortably at the top of the country's donut hierarchy. However, it wasn't always the undisputed heavyweight. In a rivalry that gives McDonald's and Burger King a run for their money, Dunkin' spent decades going head-to-head with Mister Donut. Ultimately, Dunkin' came out on top — at least, if we're talking strictly about the USA. Over in Japan, Mister Donut reigns supreme.

    What makes this feud particularly fascinating is that it was a family affair. Dunkin', originally known as Dunkin' Donuts, was founded in 1950 by William Rosenberg. The simple combination of donuts and coffee proved to be a huge success. Naturally, Rosenberg wanted to expand the business through franchising. So far, so good, right? Well, not everyone was happy with the idea, including Harry Winokur, Rosenberg's brother-in-law. In a move that would spark a decades-long rivalry, Winokur left the business and opened Mister Donut just a few miles from Dunkin's original location. He even embraced franchising, with Mister Donut employees reportedly being prohibited from saying the word "dunk" in their stores.

    As is often the case, feuds rarely end with a clear winner. In 1990, Dunkin' acquired Mister Donut and rebranded nearly all of its American locations as Dunkin' stores (ouch). Today, just one Mister Donut location remains in the U.S. That must have been a hit on Winokur's pride, but while Dunkin' was busy making cereal in the '80s, Mister Donut was thriving on the other side of the world. Today, Mister Donut is Japan's leading donut chain, with more than 900 locations in operation.

    Japan has embraced plenty of Western-style foods with open arms. Think of the juicy, hamburger-inspired hambāgu, or comforting pizza toast with its wide array of toppings. Mister Donut also happens to fit comfortably into this category. However, one thing worth knowing about Japan's take on Western staples is that they're rarely direct copies. Instead, the country has a knack for putting its own spin on imported dishes. That's exactly how Mister Donut managed to carve out a place for itself in the market.

    The first Mister Donut opened its doors in Japan in 1971, after business executive Seiichi Suzuki acquired the exclusive rights to operate the brand in the country. The original menu featured familiar American favorites, but Suzuki also introduced items and adjustments designed to appeal to local tastes. These included reducing the sugar content of certain products, serving more modest portions, and creating a cozy, sit-down atmosphere. The approach proved successful, and Mister Donut swiftly expanded across Japan. Dunkin', meanwhile, had also tried its luck in the Japanese market, opening its first location in 1970. While Mister Donut continued to grow, Dunkin' struggled to gain a foothold and eventually left Japan altogether in 1998.

    It has been revealed that in 1989, Suzuki's firm Duskin acquired full ownership of Mister Donut's Japanese operations, giving it greater freedom to develop the brand's distinctly Japanese identity. From there, the chain continued to expand, eventually bringing its donuts to markets including Thailand, Australia, Taiwan, and Singapore. Today, Mister Donut is best known for its playful, distinctly Japanese creations, particularly the Pon De Ring, a chewy, ring-shaped donut made up of small dough balls, and Mocchurin, its mochi-inspired donut line that is so soft, they require paper trays to keep each donut from losing its shape.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, the appeal of nachos is easy to understand: Cover tortilla chips with a variable mix of cheese, meat, and beans, and dig into a mouth-watering textural experience. It's a dish concept that originated in Mexico, but it has since become widely popularized in the USA, welcoming many modifications in the process. Want a version with a thick boost in flavor and texture? Make a batch of totchos, swapping the tortilla chips for miniature hash browns (aka tater tots).

    At first glance, it may seem like potatoes and nacho toppings shouldn't go together; tots are often a breakfast dish, after all. Yet the spuds make for an excellent starchy flavor canvas, ready for whatever nacho fixings you throw on. Like other loaded tater tot recipes, it's all about contrasting flavors atop a canvas of crispy potatoes.

    Sources indicate that so layer on ingredients like gooey cheese, corn and beans, flavorful ground meat or chorizo, salsa, pickled jalapeños, and more. Some bites will get a little wet, but most will remain crunchy. Yet since tater tots are much thicker than chips, the underside retains a sturdy foundation, propping up a nacho twist with a little more heft. It's among the most delicious hacks for a bag of frozen tater tots, meshing together a freezer classic item with a crowd favorite formula.

    It has been revealed that A platter of totchos fits a variety of contexts. Layer on an abundance of festive components, and the dish can be an all-out party platter. Keep it to a simple meat and cheese, and you get an affordable and comforting rendition. Whichever route you go for, construct the dish with a few considerations in mind to optimize both flavor and texture.

    When preparing the tater tots, aim for peak crunch, so cook them well before you add your toppings. A hot oven gets the job done, but consider also using the air fryer for restaurant-level crunch, or even pan-frying the tots — maybe even in chorizo fat for added flavor. Next in importance is how to incorporate the dairy, another nacho cornerstone.

    If you're making a liquidy nacho cheese sauce, you can simply drizzle the condiment onto your tots. However, if you're using shredded cheese, you'll want to melt the component on top of the tots in the oven for around five minutes. During this step, you can include already prepped ground beef taco meat, too, melding the dish components alongside the bed of potatoes.

    According to recent reports, only right before serving should you include cold ingredients. Keep it simple with chopped lettuce and onions, a light drizzle of sour cream or crema, or consider something more complex, like pico de gallo and guacamole. Cilantro and scallions are always welcome, as is a squeeze of lime. Dig in with a fork and knife (and we do suggest using cutlery — unlike with chips, you won't be easily able to grab individual tots); totchos's hearty appeal is immediate — it's the magic of nachos, with a heftier base.

    Industry News: 11 Best Classic American Candy Stores Across The US

    📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2564 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foodrepublic

    ⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • There's hardly a saying that expresses unbridled joy like "kid in a candy store." But why do kids get all the fun?
    • According to recent reports, candy has long been a staple of American culture, with the oldest candy stores in the United States stretching back into past centuries.
    • And in a society where more is more, candy stores have evolved from quaint little shops (still worth a visit for transporting yourself to the past) to mega-sized outlets overflowing with sweets.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    There's hardly a saying that expresses unbridled joy like "kid in a candy store." But why do kids get all the fun? Candy stores, those brightly colored meccas of sky-high sugar intake, beckon many Americans far into adulthood. Candy, after all, is one of those food products that can really take us back, so candy stores are capable of injecting a sense of nostalgia, childlike reverie, and excitement into anyone's day.

    According to recent reports, candy has long been a staple of American culture, with the oldest candy stores in the United States stretching back into past centuries. In the modern world, however, candy enthusiasts keep tabs on their favorite indulgences through candy-focused blogs, sweets-obsessed Instagram accounts, and TikTok viral candy sensations. Meanwhile, towns, states, and even nationwide publications regularly hold contests for the best candy store in the area (or in the country). These sources, and more, inspired this list of the coolest candy stores in the United States.

    And in a society where more is more, candy stores have evolved from quaint little shops (still worth a visit for transporting yourself to the past) to mega-sized outlets overflowing with sweets. Some have blossomed into department store-level or warehouse-like square footage, others have added attractions far beyond the candy itself, from mini golf to candy museums, and some are just old-time-tastic. The candy stores listed here are not just the perfect places to get your candy fix. They've become must-visit destinations for travelers around the country.

    Philadelphia's Shane Confectionery is one of America's oldest candy stores — in fact, it's the oldest continuously operated confectionery. The manufacturer emphasizes that this claim to fame means that its operation has been consistently making and selling confections longer than any other site in America, in a historic four-story brick building that's survived for over 150 years.

    In a recent development, but it wasn't until 1910, when the firm was sold to Edward R. Shane, that many of the retail shop's intricate, old-fashioned design elements were put into place. As the company explains, Shane installed elaborately carved cabinets, curved glass showcases, and marble countertops to highlight his confections, as well as stained glass transom windows above the storefront to allure passersby in front of his shop. Best of all, many of these architectural details have been restored and are on display in the shop today, making a visit there a bit like stepping into a charming bygone era.

    It's no wonder that Eater Philadelphia has called Shane Confectionery the "time portal to Philadelphia's sugary past," calling out the efforts of current owners, brothers Ryan and Eric Berley, who breathed latest life into the longstanding business in 2011. Fans regularly show it love online as a must-visit when living in or traveling through the City of Brotherly Love.

    110 Market St, Philadelphia, PA 19106.

    With enthusiastic reviews and a high rankings online, Sweet Pete's Candy in Jacksonville, Florida, is hailed as the largest candy store in the Southeast. And the setting can't be beat: Visit Jacksonville points out that it's located in a historic 22,000-square-foot mansion right in the heart of downtown. From sour candies to hand-pulled lollipops, Sweet Pete's has your candy cravings covered.

    Sweet Pete's Candy also gets a leg up on the candy competition by serving customers with dietary restrictions. It offers an entire allergy-friendly array of candies, including a selection of gluten-free, dairy-free, vegan-friendly, and nut-free options. A classic treat is Pete's Famous Sea Salt Caramel, now available in different flavors, like Apple Pie.

    Meanwhile, visitors can make a day out of their visit, because Sweet Pete's also houses Fizzies & Fare, an in-house restaurant and bar that's touted by the tech giant as home to hundreds of unique craft sodas, over-the-top Crazy Shakes, classic American eats, candy-inspired cocktails, and more. Candy fans can also learn how their favorite candies are made through a guided tour, led by one of the staff's "Candy Connoisseurs," through the three-story "candy mansion," then grab their own handmade custom chocolate bar fresh from Sweet Pete's kitchen. The business even hosts parties, events, field trips for local school kids, and classes on-site.

    400 N Hogan St, Jacksonville, FL 32202.

    Industry observers note that sweet Mickey's, in the Ballard neighborhood of Seattle, is named after owner Randy Brinker's grandma and pays homage to her bygone party shop and homemade sweets. Many publications laud it as one of the best candy stores in the country, thanks to its variety of homemade fudges and truffles alongside classic candy favorites like Sugar Babies and international sensations like Danish salted licorice.

    In a recent development, with a storefront tucked into the charming brick buildings of historic Ballard, it's the perfect place for a candy store with a vintage vibe and an old-time Americana aesthetic. From handmade goodies to its carefully curated selection of traditional and artisanal sweets from around the globe, candy lovers (or even the pickiest of eaters) can find something for them.

    Even better, this candy store has a heart. Since its 2012 grand opening, it has supported the local Little League, sponsored movie nights in the park, and hosted onsite parties and events to create sweet memories and build community.

    5338 Ballard Ave NW, Seattle, WA 98107.

    It'Sugar, with candy-colored locations nationwide, was already known for its San Francisco flagship location, with a three-floor candy store in Fisherman's Wharf. The brand, with locations from coast to coast, then opened a 24,000-square-foot location in East Rutherford, New Jersey's American Dream shopping mall. This location, dubbed the World's First Candy Department Store, also spans three floors, though there are plenty across the country.

    Some of its over-the-top features at the East Rutherford location include: a three-story-tall Statue of Liberty replica covered in more than 1.5 million Jelly Belly beans, an immersive lollipop garden filled with nearly 10,000 lollipops, dozens of branded shops like Sour Patch Kids, Swedish Fish, Nerds, Starburst, and Reese's. It's truly a candy lover's dream come true. YouTubers have hailed it as an amazing feat of candy awesomeness, all a stone's throw from Newly introduced York City.

    The brand It'Sugar calls itself a "retailtainer," a mashup of retailer and entertainment. As manufacturer lore explains, the brand was founded by candy veteran Jeff Rubin in 2006 and has grown to more than 120 locations throughout the United States and Canada. It's known for "absurd sugar innovations" and the Sugar High Club, with which loyal visitors can earn points for their purchases — then, of course, they can cash them in for more sugar.

    Recent findings suggest that cleveland hosts North America's largest candy store, going strong for more than 75 years: b.a. Sweetie Candy Organization. Cleveland.com calls it Cleveland's version of Willy Wonka's Candy Factory, and for good reason. Company stats boast that it hosts more than 500,000 visitors per year (making it one of the city's top attractions) and stocks more than 5,500 items in its wholesale store, to the tune of over $5 million in inventory on-hand at any given time.

    According to recent reports, with classic candy, retro candy, bulk candy, wholesale candy, and more, the store promises "the absolute largest variety of candy available anywhere in North America." Meaning, if you need 1,000 pounds of Tootsie Rolls to throw a parade, it's your outlet. It even keeps an eye on bygone favorites and claims it has been instrumental in bringing back vintage candies that had disappeared from shelves, including nostalgic names like Bonomo's Turkish Taffy, Slo Poke, Regal Crown, and Broadway licorice rolls.

    All that would be enough to lure any candy fan, but b.a. Sweetie Candy Company is much more than just a candy store. It's a bona fide family-fun destination, offering Golfland Park, which has two 18-hole mini golf courses, complete with lights for evening play, koi ponds, a cascading waterfall, and concession stands. Meanwhile, the Soda Shoppe serves up homemade ice cream, sundaes, malts, and over 100 sodas in a barn-style parlor.

    6770 Brookpark Rd, Cleveland, OH 44129.

    In a recent development, this Latest York City treasure actually started as a shoe and hat repair shop — but a little push cart outside also sold candy. According to company lore, in the Depression years, 1937, the business owners decided to focus on their biggest moneymaker, candy, and became known as Economy Candy. After World War II, Morris "Moishe" Cohen and his brother in law assumed ownership and expanded the business, selling candy, chocolate, gift baskets, dried fruit, nuts, and more. Morris' son, Jerry, and his wife, Ilene, took over after its move to the current location at 108 Rivington Street, then passed the business to son Mitchell, who runs it today.

    Sources indicate that in other words, this living legend is a true family affair — and a multigenerational sensation that has become a part of the rich history of Fresh York City. In 2023, the northwest corner of Rivington and Essex Streets were co-named Morris "Moishe" Cohen Way in honor of Morris and Economy Candy's lasting legacies.

    Today, the store still boasts over 2,000 items for sale, and visitors routinely rave about its massive selection and reasonable prices online. Hot sellers include chocolate-covered graham crackers (with and without jelly), chocolate-covered pretzels, jelly rings, gummies, and those hard-to-find candy bars. For those outside Latest York City, Economy Candy offers online sales, as well.

    108 Rivington St, New York, NY 10002.

    Sources indicate that A candy shop with old-fashioned soda fountain treats like ice cream, specialty chocolate candies and fudge, more than 400 candies for buying in bulk, and 3,000-plus wrapped candies — all in colorful circus-theme surroundings? Yes, please.

    The Massive Top Candy Shop has been serving the Austin community (as well as candy-minded travelers) since 2007. Visitors praised its wall-to-wall candy selection, laid out in candy-colored rows, jars, racks, and even in a lollipop tree. Passing by Peanuts, the elephant pictured on the shop's entrance (facing the city's famed South Congress Avenue, known for housing quirky boutiques), visitors will find a whimsical wonderland at Big Top Candy with classic soda machines, retro candies, and a hefty bulk section customers can grab by the scoop.

    The store promises both nostalgic favorites and newly introduced creations from around the globe. Whether you're just passing through for SXSW or a stalwart resident, Significant Top Candy Shop is a must-visit in the Live Music Capital of the World.

    1706 S Congress Ave, Austin, TX 78704.

    Minnesota's Largest Candy Store in Jordan, Minnesota, nods to its mind-boggling mass of inventory in its very name — and the company would seem intent on living up to that moniker. Owned by Robert Wagner, and also known as Jim's Apple Farm, the store houses not only nostalgic candy, but fresh-baked pies and strudels, the world's largest selection of sodas, an array of popcorn flavors, and locally-sourced items (think pastas, jams, jellies, and even puzzles). These are all sourced from surrounding farms, making this Midwestern gem not only a candy emporium but a true shopping destination that supports locals and promotes Minnesota products to everyone who enters.

    Fortunately, its location is relatively convenient for passers-through, as the store is only 35 miles from Minneapolis. And you can't miss it — the store is housed in a massive, bright yellow barn. It's a must-stop not only thanks to its dizzying array of sweet and savory treats, but fun touches throughout its interior decor, such as a new observatory-like dome featuring a mural with more than two dozen superheroes, an animatronic band, and a fortune-telling machine. Essentially, this Minnesota behemoth will bring out the kid in anyone.

    minnesotaslargestcandystore.com.

    20430 Johnson Memorial Dr, Jordan, MN 55352.

    Sources indicate that calling itself one of the oldest continuously operated, family-owned candy businesses in the U.S., Schimpff's Confectionery has been hailed as America's best candy store. It was also featured on a national television special "Disney Celebrates America: The Pursuit of Happiness.".

    According to recent reports, with 135 years of history, Schimpff's Confectionery more than deserves those honors — its recipes and business stretch back to the 1800s. The company history notes that the recipe for its famous Cinnamon Red Hots were handwritten in the recipe book of Gustav "Gus" Schimpff Sr. back in 1891. And it's still making waves, having been featured on several reveals and publications.

    With such an illustrious history, it makes sense that Schimpff's Confectionery also houses a candy museum, with thousands of pieces of American candy memorabilia. The museum, along with a candy demonstration area, were added to an adjacent building in 2001, a dream child of 1990s-era owners Warren Schimpff and his wife Jill. Today, fifth-generation owners Steve and Beth Shepherd have taken the helm and embrace the time-honored traditions and recipes at Schimpff's Confectionery.

    347 Spring St, Jeffersonville, IN 47130.

    According to recent reports, seeking candy from the 1970s, or maybe your favorite candy from the 1990s? The Peppermint Stick Candy Store & Ice Cream Parlor in Boyertown, Pennsylvania, stocks a cornucopia of vintage candies alongside modern-day favorites and gourmet goodies like truffles. Whether you're visiting in-store or shopping online, this candy store has got you covered. In fact, its website has a handy online shopping feature, making it easy for customers to browse by decade.

    It has been revealed that opened in 2015, this woman-owned business also offers Longacre's ice cream for indulgent sundaes and 20-ounce milkshakes, plus bakery delights like Ice Cream Nachos (waffle cones make the chips) and the Cinnamon Roll Sundae, and a Soda Jerk menu with soda fountain favorites. Customers will find not just a store, but an unforgettable experience at The Peppermint Stick Candy Store & Ice Cream Parlor. They can find fudge, artisan chocolates, loose chocolates, gummy candy, penny candy, nostalgic candy, gourmet truffles (in flavors like mint, Champagne, tiramisu, and key lime), and even a penny candy section. Basically, if you leave hungry, you've done something wrong.

    26 E Philadelphia Ave, Boyertown, PA 19512.

    Recent findings suggest that since 1934, Bright's Candies has been whipping up candy the old-fashioned way. Even now, this destination features charming equipment to make its treats, including large copper kettles, metal candy molds, and an antique popcorn popper in its candy kitchen. Even better, the viewing windows in the shop are designed to give everyone a front row look at the process, allowing kids and adults to watch the staff confectioners at work. All of these factors contribute to an impressively high Yelp rating, where customers called it cute and charming, with a heavenly smell and friendly staff members.

    It has been revealed that this candy store won national recognition for its sweet treats, and for decades, has been known for wafting aromas of caramel corn and waffle cones down Walla Walla's Main Street. Try out the chocolates, truffles, and seasonal items like handmade chocolate Easter bunnies. Or, go for fudge, licorice, or colorful frozen treats. In other words, it's not just a candy store; it's a place to immerse all of your senses in sweets. What's not to love about that?

    11 E Main St, Walla Walla, WA 99362.

    This list was compiled using review sites like Reddit, Google, and Tripadvisor; research on candy stores' websites from coast to coast; and tracking media mentions on major news outlets. Extra attention was given to candy stores that are historic and/or boast unique offerings to visitors, such as mini golf, soda fountains, museums, and more.

    #10512. Forget Plain Butter: Drizzle This Rich Ingredient Over Stuffing For 10x The Flavor

    📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (541 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foodrepublic ↗ Open Full Page

    Forget Plain Butter: Drizzle This Rich Ingredient Over Stuffing For 10x The Flavor

    📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (541 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foodrepublic

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When it comes to the Thanksgiving feast, Americans' favorite sides include mashed potatoes, green bean casserole, and of course, stuffing.
    • Recent findings suggest that brown butter is most notably used in sweet baked goods, but the golden, nutty version can truly enhance pretty much anything where regular butter is used, including savory dishes like stuffing.
    • In a recent development, don't skimp on it, either.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When it comes to the Thanksgiving feast, Americans' favorite sides include mashed potatoes, green bean casserole, and of course, stuffing. Whether it comes from a box or is lovingly homemade, stuffing is a filling, savory, and surprisingly historical part of many Turkey Day spreads. And there are seemingly as many variations of stuffing as there are households in the U.S., but butter is a unifying and necessary ingredient that no version of this Thanksgiving side can go without. However, if you really want to up the richness and flavor of your next casserole dish of stuffing, forget plain old regular butter and instead try brown butter.

    Recent findings suggest that brown butter is most notably used in sweet baked goods, but the golden, nutty version can truly enhance pretty much anything where regular butter is used, including savory dishes like stuffing. What it adds to your T-giving side is a sumptuous, caramelly flavor that creates a world of depth and complexity, as the sweetness of the brown butter beautifully complements all the savory ingredients in the stuffing, like the softened bread cubes, sausage (if you use any), and the fresh herbs.

    In a recent development, don't skimp on it, either. If you're going to use brown butter in stuffing, you'll need to start with quite a bit of butter, perhaps as much as two to three full sticks, because the flavors in your typical stuffing can be bold, and you want to be able to taste the butterscotch-y nuttiness, which pairs so well with sage and onion, or the mushroom in a classic sausage and mushroom stuffing. Even if you make a pumpkin and herb stuffing, full of warming spices and chili, brown butter will enhance the subtle sweetness of the pumpkin and the juiciness of the raisins.

    If you're inspired to try using brown butter in your stuffing this year for Thanksgiving, but you've never made it before and you're a little intimidated by it, we've a few tips to get you started. First thing, the color of the pan you use matters because you'll want to keep a close eye on how dark the butter is getting — hard to do in cast iron. The choice is yours whether you use salted or unsalted butter, but you'll want to adjust the seasonings in your stuffing accordingly. It's important that you don't use too high a heat; a good medium to medium-low will do the trick. And finally, don't walk away while your butter is browning because the process is quick, and you can go from delectably golden brown with a nutty aroma to burnt and bitter in a hurry.

    There are a number of ways to incorporate brown butter into your stuffing, and whichever you choose, you'll want to remove the pan off the heat as soon as the butter is ready. You might add the veggies, aromatics, and herbs directly into the brown butter pan and let those saturate and saute in the nutty goodness, then add them to the bread element. Or you can remove the brown butter from the pan and keep it aside in a bowl, saute the vegetables, add everything into the waiting bowl of butter, and toss to combine.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that when you need protein to help support your body after a workout or to keep you satiated throughout the day, you can reach for a number of foods, but we'd venture that there isn't a tastier option than a hamburger or cheeseburger. There are plenty of fast food options that are positively awash in the macronutrient, but cooking at home gives you far more control. Now, ground beef is obviously chock-full of protein, with anywhere from 16 to 24 grams per 4-ounce serving, but if you have a serious goal you need to meet before EOD, there is a canned ingredient that is probably lurking in your pantry (and if it isn't, it should be) that can help push you over the edge. It's beans!

    Depending on the type of bean you use, a half-cup typically contains between 7 and 9 grams of protein that you can add to your meat mixture, and ultimately, black beans would be our first choice. Not only are they closest in color to a perfectly grilled burger, but they're surprisingly meaty. When they're mashed and mixed in with the ground beef, they blend right in, and their mild flavor means they take on whatever seasonings you include without drawing attention to themselves (oh, and there's the added bonus that, in addition to the extra protein, they're also a high-fiber food). By the way, if you don't have black beans on hand, you can absolutely use pinto, cannellini, or even red kidney beans.

    Recent findings suggest that canned beans are often packed in a gooey liquid that consists of the starches and other substances that seep out of the beans, mixed with water and sometimes a bit of salt. As such, they are too wet straight out of the can to use in your burger mixture, so you should drain them and then dry them as much as you can (otherwise, your patties could be a soggy mess). You can even help the process by wicking as much moisture out of them as possible, making for a much more desirable texture, by placing them in a single layer on a baking sheet and popping them in the oven for a few minutes.

    Mashing the beans by hand before adding them to the ground beef will always be preferable to the evisceration they'd receive in a food processor. Taking a potato masher (or you could use your meat chopper from the Dollar Tree) to the beans produces a variety of different shapes, which is useful not just for aesthetic purposes (the irregularities in the beans mimic the natural lumps that form when burger patties cook), but also for a more satisfyingly hearty bite.

    Recent findings suggest that now, beans and ground beef alone do not a burger patty make; you may want to include some binders to help hold everything together. This might be as simple as an egg or two and breadcrumbs — which type of breadcrumbs is totally up to you, because typical fine-textured crumbs will work, as will panko — plus a condiment of your choice, like ketchup, mustard, or even tangy barbecue sauce.

    For The Best Scrambled Eggs With Extra Fiber, Make Them Turkish Style

    📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (509 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foodrepublic

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Getting your morning fiber doesn't have to be all about eating more fruits or specialty yogurts.
    • Recent findings suggest that A proper menemen is customizable, but always requires three things: eggs, tomatoes, and peppers.
    • According to recent reports, this is without even mentioning the fiber in the peppers.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Getting your morning fiber doesn't have to be all about eating more fruits or specialty yogurts. Instead, you can deliciously upgrade your scrambled eggs with classic Turkish vegetables in menemen, a sort of low-effort dish that comes loaded with nutrients.

    Recent findings suggest that A proper menemen is customizable, but always requires three things: eggs, tomatoes, and peppers. It lets you get so much fiber because it starts with sauteing the vegetables until they soften and reduce in size, so you can load up quite a bit in a single meal. While the exact nutritional profile varies between different types of tomatoes, there's an average of about 2.16 grams of fiber per cup. The sauteing step means you can easily add two cups and cook them down to a thick, jammy consistency, providing a delicious brightness to the eggs just over 4 grams of fiber all in one go.

    According to recent reports, this is without even mentioning the fiber in the peppers. Banana peppers are relatively high in fiber, clocking in at around 4 grams per cup. Bell peppers are also quite tasty, with some varieties providing about 3 grams per cup. Since the recommended daily fiber intake for most adults hovers between 25 and 38 grams, you could potentially get a substantial portion of your daily needs all in one go. And unlike shakshuka and eggs in purgatory, two similar dishes that traditionally rely on poaching or braising, menemen lets you control the texture quite easily, whether you like your eggs creamy, fluffy, or dense.

    Between the rich flavors of menemen and the plethora of foods it can pair with, you've got ample room to deliciously add even more fiber to your breakfast. Taking inspiration from a traditional Turkish breakfast is a great place to start, but don't be afraid to treat your menemen as a starting point rather than a set-in-stone recipe.

    In a recent development, like many countries, Turkey is a big believer in some early morning carbs, and bread products are a great way to add a bit more fiber to your diet. While a slice of white bread may be versatile and provide some sweetness to round out the tomatoes' acidity, one slice also only has about 0.6 grams of fiber. Instead, look to rye, a bread that may not be for everyone but can have three times the fiber of white bread. A slice of pumpernickel can even add 2.7 more grams of fiber to your morning, and the rich, earthy aromas and dense texture are a great contrast to creamy eggs and veggies.

    Few fruits are quite so high in fiber as avocado, with a single medium-sized fruit containing around 10 grams of fiber. As a topping for menemen, its rich creaminess works perfectly with the sharper vegetable flavors, while the eggs provide plenty of protein. Half an avocado smeared over pumpernickel and topped with menemen could provide around 16 grams of fiber from all the different sources, roughly half of what many people need per day.

    The Chain Italian Sub With The Best Bread, According To Customer Reviews

    📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (467 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Foodrepublic

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Italian sub sandwiches are a thing of beauty: cured meats piled high, creamy cheese, a bit of lettuce and tomato, perhaps a slather of mayo if you're feeling controversial, and maybe a drizzle of herb-infused oil and vinegar.
    • For example, one Reddit user shared that DiBella's version of an Italian, called the Godfather, did not disappoint.
    • Another reviewer on Yelp also specifically cited the Godfather, saying it was extremely flavorful.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Italian sub sandwiches are a thing of beauty: cured meats piled high, creamy cheese, a bit of lettuce and tomato, perhaps a slather of mayo if you're feeling controversial, and maybe a drizzle of herb-infused oil and vinegar. You can find them at pretty much any sandwich shop or deli, though naturally, a number of factors, like size and overall quality, will vary. And while the meats and cheese might be the stars of the show, you cannot discount the importance of good bread. According to a Food Republic roundup of the 10 best chain Italian subs, Upcoming York-based chain DiBella's stood out on account of just that, with customers particularly praising its signature everything bread, which adds an extra layer of savory flavor thanks to its topping of seasonings, including ingredients like garlic, poppy seeds, and sesame seeds.

    For example, one Reddit user shared that DiBella's version of an Italian, called the Godfather, did not disappoint. "The 'everything' bread was the best part [in my opinion]," they wrote, "but the whole sub was pretty [top-tier] as far as chain restaurants go.".

    Another reviewer on Yelp also specifically cited the Godfather, saying it was extremely flavorful. "[It] was ridiculously good. So much flavor and taste. The bread really sealed the deal," they praised.

    Recent findings suggest that if the glowing reviews have you hankering for a sandwich from a chain you've never heard of before, you're not alone. The reason DiBella's mostly flies under the radar is that it is actually quite limited in locations. As of November 2026, the chain is only present in five states, with the majority of its locations concentrated in New York, its home state, and Ohio. And for the first 80 years of its existence (DiBella's was founded in 1918 as a grocery store), it consisted of just one Rochester location. That changed in 1998, when the company opened its second location, and since then, DiBella's has seen a flurry of expansion, with 2024 proving especially busy.

    However, the smaller chain size might actually contribute to the quality of the bread that has put DiBella's on the map, since fewer locations make it easier to maintain standards. For now, in all 44 of the sandwich shop's restaurants, the bread gets baked at least twice daily, as the final step in a process that takes more than half a day. Before the rolls go in the oven, though, the dough gets aged for a minimum of 16 hours to improve texture and taste. Then, seasonings are manually sprinkled on top, and finally, someone wielding a knife hand-scores the tops of the loaves. The frequency of this baking process means that you will almost assuredly get sub rolls at their peak freshness whenever you place your order at DiBella's.

    Olive Garden's Buttery Breadstick Topping Is Actually Dairy-Free

    📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (524 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foodrepublic

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Many diners would agree that one of the biggest pleasures of dining out at Olive Garden isn't just the ambiance or even the appetizers or entrees, like the Tour of Italy, but rather one of the complimentary items that comes with your meal: breadsticks.
    • In a recent development, margarine differs from butter in that it is made from oils with a variety of additional ingredients, including water.
    • It has been revealed that butter can also resolidify after it cools, potentially giving the breadsticks a pasty coating.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Many diners would agree that one of the biggest pleasures of dining out at Olive Garden isn't just the ambiance or even the appetizers or entrees, like the Tour of Italy, but rather one of the complimentary items that comes with your meal: breadsticks. These soft, pillowy sticks of dough are buttery, garlicky, and great for dipping into dressing or sauces. They are so popular that the chain of Italian-inspired restaurants goes through a staggering number each week, and many diners may even request some extra when taking home leftovers. But despite the buttery flavor of this signature item, it doesn't actually contain any real butter. Instead, the company uses margarine.

    In a recent development, margarine differs from butter in that it is made from oils with a variety of additional ingredients, including water. Together, they form an emulsion that can resemble butter. While not all brands of margarine are completely dairy-free, the kind Olive Garden uses doesn't contain any dairy at all, making it suitable for diners with dairy allergies or those who abstain from animal-derived foods. One reason Olive Garden may use margarine instead of butter is that it can provide a smoother, more consistent topping for its breadsticks.

    It has been revealed that butter can also resolidify after it cools, potentially giving the breadsticks a pasty coating. According to Reddit consumers, Olive Garden uses liquid margarine, which retains its consistency. Additionally, margarine is generally less expensive than butter, and in an industry with razor-thin margins, anywhere you can save money can lead to greater profits.

    Perhaps the best use of margarine for Olive Garden fans is to recreate a homemade version of its iconic breadsticks. You can start by using Great Value Garlic Bread Sticks — a fantastic store-bought dupe, available at Walmart — and brushing melted margarine over the sticks after they're heated for an extra buttery finish. Or you can use the melted margarine to give upcoming life to any of the chain's leftover breadsticks you bring home.

    Margarine's uses extend well beyond breadsticks, though. For starters, many types of margarine retain a soft texture even when refrigerated, meaning you can easily spread it onto bread or toast even when it's cold. Try doing that with regular butter! Because some types of margarine contain little to no milk solids, they also don't burn as easily as traditional butter does. This means that you can use them to pan-fry foods at relatively higher temperatures than you can with butter without as much risk of altering the flavor of the finished dish.

    Recent findings suggest that finally, margarine is also great for baking. You can often use it in place of butter in the same quantities, though the substitution may affect the finished product. Certain types of margarine also remain solid at higher temperatures, which can be beneficial when baking things like pastries, where fat that melts too quickly can make the difference between beautiful, puffy layers and a flat, greasy end result. Just be sure to avoid spreads or squeezable margarine for baking, as the water content can be too high and negatively affect your recipe.

    Breaking: How I Get Free Traffic from ChatGPT in 2025 (AIO vs SEO)
